en: Arjuna said:
O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and yet again, you praise yoga.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better. //1//
Śrīdhara:
Having dispelled Arjuna’s doubt regarding the yoga of action and the yoga of renunciation,
[the Lord] declared liberation for the self-controlled ascetic in the fifth chapter.
It was stated: "Having cut through the doubt born of ignorance with the sword of knowledge, take recourse in the yoga of action.
Regarding this, Arjuna, perceiving a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, said: "Renunciation...
[He means: By such passages as "But he who rejoices only in the Self," and "All action in its entirety, O Pārtha," you speak of the renunciation of action.
Having cut through doubt with the sword of knowledge, "abide in yoga"—thus you speak again of yoga.

Yet, the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*) and the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) cannot both belong to one and the same person at the same time, because their essential natures are contradictory.
Therefore, since only one of these two must be practiced, tell me that one which is most certainly the better for me. //1//
Madhusūdana:
Through these two chapters, the determination of action and knowledge has been established;
now, the determination of action and its renunciation is being made through the [next] two chapters.

In the third chapter, having been questioned by Arjuna with the words "If you consider knowledge superior to action," and so forth, the Blessed One established the definitive conclusion through the distinction of different types of qualified practitioners— since neither option nor combination of knowledge and action is possible— beginning with the verse: "O sinless one, in this world, two kinds of steadfastness were declared by Me in the past."

Likewise, action pertaining to the sphere of injunction is not combined with knowledge, because the two cannot exist simultaneously— like light and darkness— since knowledge, by dispelling the notion of difference that is the cause for the qualification to perform action, stands in opposition to it. Nor can they be treated as optional alternatives, because they lack a single common purpose.

Because the destruction of ignorance, which is the effect of knowledge, cannot be accomplished by action—according to the Śruti: "Only by knowing Him does one pass over death; there is no other path for the journey"—once knowledge has arisen, the effect of action is simply not required, as stated in the passage beginning, "As much purpose as there is in a small reservoir. Thus, since it is certain that the knower has no further qualification for ritual action, his engagement with it—whether as a mere futile exertion due to the force of *prārabdha*-karma, or as the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of all actions—is established beyond dispute in the Fourth [Book].
This has been determined.

However, for one who is ignorant, ritual actions must be performed as a means to purify the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) so that knowledge may arise, according to the Vedic scripture: "Brahmins seek to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting."
And because of the Lord’s own words: "O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge.
Thus, all actions are for the sake of knowledge;
likewise, the renunciation of all actions is also heard in scripture to be for the sake of knowledge: "Desiring this very world, mendicants go forth into the homeless life."
Being peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed, one should see the Self in the very self;
for that which is to be known is to be abandoned by the abandoner alone, as the supreme state is inward-facing, transcending both truth and falsehood, and pleasure and pain.

In such passages as, "Having abandoned these Vedas, this world, and the next, one should seek the Self," there can be no combination (*samuccaya*) of ritual action and its abandonment— whether as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) or as directly contributing auxiliaries (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)— just as there is none between the *prayāja* offerings and the threshing of grain, because they are contradictory and cannot coexist simultaneously.

Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) between ritual action and its abandonment on the grounds that they both have the single fruit of self-knowledge, as in the case of the optional taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *atirātra* sacrifice.
Because there is no identity of purpose due to the difference in their respective means:
for action, the means is indeed the unseen (adṛṣṭa) result consisting of the destruction of sin;
but for renunciation, the means is the seen (dṛṣṭa) one, consisting of providing an opportunity for inquiry through the absence of all distractions.

The transcendental result (*apūrva*) arising from a restrictive rule (*niyama*), however, is not a motivator [for the performance of an action], because it is directly connected to a visible purpose, as in the case of threshing and so forth.

Thus, even though the invisible-purpose and visible-purpose factors—the remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) and the proximate auxiliary (*saṃnipātyopakāraka*)—both serve a single primary purpose, there is no optionality (*vikalpa*) between them at all;
otherwise, it would follow that there would likewise be optionality for the *prayāja* offerings, the threshing, and so on.
Therefore, both [renunciation and action] should be practiced in sequence.

Even in that case, if one were to perform ritual action immediately after renunciation, then by re-accepting a previous stage of life (āśrama) that had been abandoned, one would become a "fallen one" (patita) who has descended from a higher state; consequently, there would be no eligibility for ritual action, and the prior renunciation would be rendered futile because it would lack its intended transcendental purpose (adṛṣṭārtha).
If the qualification for knowledge were obtained merely by the initial renunciation, then the performance of ritual action thereafter would be useless.
Therefore, first, through the performance of desireless action with the intention of offering it to the Lord, when the internal organ is purified and intense dispassion arises,
once the desire to know (vividiṣā) has become firm, the renunciation of all actions is undertaken for the purpose of investigating the Vedānta texts through hearing, reflection, and so forth.
"It must be performed"—this is the Blessed One's view.
And so it has been said: "By the non-commencement of actions, a person does not attain freedom from action (naiṣkarmya).
And it will be stated further:
"For one who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means" (Gītā 6.3).
Here, "yoga" refers to the desire to know (vividiṣā) preceded by intense dispassion.
This has been stated by the authors of the Vārttika: "The study of the Vedas and other such practices are for the sake of accomplishing the desire to know the Inner Self;
but for the attainment of Brahman, their renunciation is required, by the force of the Śruti which says, 'They desire [Brahman]'."
And the Smṛti says:
"The series of impurities are the actions, but knowledge is the supreme goal;
when the impurities have been ripened by actions, then knowledge arises."
In the *Mokṣadharma*: "Having ripened his impurities (*kaṣāya*) through the three stages of the ladder,
he should go forth into the supreme state, the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*)."
And through the instruments [of action] belonging to future lives, this pure-souled one attains liberation indeed in the first stage of life across many wombs of saṃsāra.
"But for the wise man who has attained that [liberation] and seen the goal,
what indeed could be the most desired object among the three stages of life? Here, "liberation" (mokṣa) means dispassion (vairāgya).
By this, both gradual renunciation and immediate renunciation are shown.
And so says the Śruti: "Having completed the stage of studentship, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller, and from there go forth;
or otherwise, one may go forth directly from studentship, or from the home, or from the forest. On whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should go forth."
Therefore, for the ignorant person, there is only the performance of ritual action during the state of non-detachment;

for that same person, however, there is renunciation during the state of detachment, which serves the purpose of attaining knowledge by providing the opportunity for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. Thus, the fifth and sixth chapters are commenced to explain the performance of action and its abandonment with reference specifically to the ignorant person, according to the distinction between these two states.

As for the renunciation of the wise (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*), since it is established as a matter of course through the power of knowledge, it is not examined here because there is no doubt regarding it. In this context, however, since both the performance of action and its abandonment have been taught by me for the sake of knowledge to the single seeker who is ignorant, and since these two are contradictory and cannot be practiced simultaneously, [the seeker wonders]: "What should be performed now by me, who am a seeker?"

Doubting, Arjuna said: "Renunciation," O Kṛṣṇa— O you whose nature is eternal bliss, or rather, O you who draw away the suffering of your devotees— [I ask about] the renunciation, that is, the abandonment, of actions such as those prescribed by the Vedas for as long as one lives, including both the obligatory (nitya) and the occasional (naimittika) rites.

To an ignorant person desiring knowledge, you speak by means of the Vedas; yet, conversely, you praise Yoga in the form of the performance of ritual action through two sets of scriptural statements, such as: "Desiring this very world, mendicants renounce their homes," and "Brahmins seek to know that very Self through the recitation of the Vedas and through sacrifice."

"Free from desire, with mind and self controlled, having renounced all possessions, performing action only for the body, he incurs no sin. (Gītā 4.21). Or, by the two verses of the Gītā: "Having cut asunder this doubt, take refuge in yoga; arise, O Bhārata! (Gītā 4.42).

In this regard, since both action and its renunciation are prescribed for the ignorant person, and since it is impossible to practice both simultaneously, tell me with certainty which one you consider superior between these two— action or its renunciation— for the purpose of my own practice. //1//
Viśvanātha:
It has been stated that action is superior even to knowledge for the sake of achieving firmness in that [knowledge];
and the knowledge of the meaning of those words is equal [to it] in the fifth [chapter].
Anticipating a contradiction based on the statement heard at the end of the previous chapter, he asks: "Renunciation... [referring to Gītā 5.1]:
"O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been rent asunder by knowledge, and who is self-possessed. (Gītā 4.41)
By this statement, you teach the renunciation of action for one in whom knowledge has arisen through the yoga of action.
Therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt residing in the heart, which is born of ignorance, take recourse in yoga; arise, O Bhārata! (Gītā 4.42)
By this [statement], you further speak of both the renunciation of action and the yoga of action for that very same person;

yet neither the renunciation of action nor the yoga of action can possibly exist for one and the same person at one and the same time, because their essential natures are as contradictory as staying still and moving.

Therefore, not having understood your intention as to whether one who possesses knowledge should practice the renunciation of action (karma-saṃnyāsa) or the yoga of action (karma-yoga), I ask you: tell me which one of these two you have determined to be the better. //1//

Baladeva says: In the fifth [chapter], Hari stated that knowledge is superior to action because it is easier to perform and so forth, and that for one who is pure, there is non-agency with respect to that [action], and so on.
In the second chapter, having declared that self-knowledge is the liberator for one desiring liberation, [the Lord] taught that desireless action must be performed as a means to that knowledge.
Then, in the third chapter, He stated that for one who has attained such knowledge there is no action at all, saying "he should be one who finds delight only in the Self";
and in the fourth chapter, He said, "All action in its entirety, O Pārtha..."
But previously, with the words beginning "Therefore, that which has arisen from ignorance" (Gītā 4.42), You spoke again of *karma-yoga* for that very same person.
Regarding this, Arjuna asks: "Renunciation," O Kṛṣṇa!
The meaning is that you praise the renunciation of actions—which consists in the cessation of the activity of all the senses—as the yoga of knowledge;
yet you also praise yoga, which is the performance of action consisting in the activity of all the senses.
And these two cannot possibly coexist for one person at the same time.
Because they are of contradictory natures, like stillness and motion, or like darkness and light; therefore,
being unable to discern whether one who has attained knowledge should renounce action or continue to perform it— according to your own view— I ask which of these two,
the renunciation of action or the performance of action, is superior.
"Tell me the reality that has been well-ascertained by you. //1//
The Blessed Lord said: Both renunciation and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good.
But of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action. //2//
Śrīdhara: To this, the Blessed Lord spoke the reply beginning with "renunciation" (saṃnyāsa).
The meaning is this: I do not prescribe the yoga of action for one who knows the reality of the Self as it is to be known through the Vedānta;
for that would be in contradiction with the renunciation mentioned previously.

Rather, I say this to you, who identify the body with the self: having severed with the sword of knowledge that discriminates the body from the self this very doubt caused by grief, delusion, and the like arising from the slaughter of kinsmen and so forth, take recourse in Karma-yoga, which serves as the means for the knowledge of the Supreme Self.

It was previously stated that once the knowledge of the true nature of the self has arisen in one whose mind is purified through Karma-yoga, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is prescribed as a limb of the steadfastness in knowledge (jñāna-niṣṭhā) for the sake of its further maturation.

This being the case, since there is an option between the subordinate and the principal, both renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the yoga of action (karma-yoga) together—according to the distinction of stages—accomplish the supreme good. Nevertheless, between those two, the yoga of action is superior to renunciation of action. //2//
Madhusūdana:
To this question of Arjuna, the Blessed Lord spoke this reply beginning with the words "Renunciation" (sannyāsa).
These two bring about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) because, by being causes for the arising of knowledge, they are conducive to liberation.
But between those two, karma-yoga is superior to the renunciation of action performed by one who lacks qualification, because it brings about the attainment of qualification. //2//
Viśvanātha:
Since it is said that "the yoga of action is superior," there is no fault whatsoever in the wise person performing action;
on the contrary, through the purification and stabilization of the mind by means of desireless action, there will indeed be a strengthening of knowledge.
But for a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), when a deficiency of the mind (citta-vaiguṇya) occasionally occurs, what action is forbidden for the sake of pacifying it?
The deficiency of the mind is indeed an obstacle to the practice of knowledge (jñānābhyāsa).
The sense is that in grasping at sense objects, there would be nothing but the act of eating one's own vomit. //2//

Baladeva: Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said: "Renunciation" (saṃnyāsa) refers to those two which bring about the highest good—that is, the causes of liberation. Renunciation of action is superior; it becomes more excellent than the yoga of knowledge.
The meaning is this: indeed, even for one who has attained knowledge, the yoga of action (karma-yoga) is not detrimental;
rather, because it is pregnant with knowledge, it serves only to strengthen that knowledge.

However, for the renunciant of action (karma-sannyāsin) who is established in knowledge, if a defect of the mind should arise, action must be performed in order to destroy that defect, according to the prohibitive scriptures.
The statements regarding the renunciation of action, however, mean that when one is established in the Self, actions themselves abandon him.
Therefore, because it is easy to perform, because it is free from negligence, and because it contains knowledge within it, Karma-yoga is superior. //2//
He should be known as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires; for, O mighty-armed one, being free from the pairs of opposites, he is easily liberated from bondage. (5.3)

Śrīdhara: In response to the question "Why?", he praises the Karma-yogin by virtue of his being a renunciant (saṃnyāsin) and demonstrates his superiority, saying: "He is to be known as such. He who performs actions for the sake of the Supreme Lord, free from attachment, aversion, and the like, is to be known as a renunciant even at the time of constantly performing those actions. The reason for this is that one who is free from the pairs of opposites—void of the dualities of attachment and aversion and so forth—and whose mind is pure, is liberated from the bondage of saṃsāra easily and without effort through the gateway of knowledge. //3//
Madhusūdana:
He praises that very yoga of action with three verses beginning with "jñeya.
Even though engaged in action, he should be known as a perpetual renunciant (saṃnyāsī).
Who is he? He who does not hate [action] performed with the understanding that it is offered to the Blessed One, out of fear that it might be fruitless;
nor does he desire heaven and so forth.

For, O mighty-armed one, being free from the pairs of opposites—meaning devoid of attachment and aversion—he easily, without effort, [is released] from bondage, which consists of the impurity of the internal organ.
One is liberated from the obstruction to knowledge; that is, one becomes freed through the excellence of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, and so forth. //3//
Viśvanātha:
Nor should it be said that liberation, which is attainable through renunciation, cannot be attained by one who has not performed renunciation; thus he says, "is to be known.
That practitioner of action whose mind is purified should indeed be known as a perpetual renunciant.
"O mighty-armed one"—the implication is that he alone is the great hero capable of conquering the city of liberation. //3//
Baladeva: To the question "In what way is he distinguished?", he says: "He is to be known.
That practitioner of karma-yoga who possesses a purified mind is a perpetual renunciant;
he is always to be known as one established in jñāna-yoga.
He who is completely satisfied by the bliss of experiencing the Self inherent within action desires nothing else nor hates anything.
Being free from the pairs of opposites yet enduring them, he attains happiness without effort; the meaning is that this is achieved through steadfastness in easily performed action. //3//
The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
even by being properly established in one, a person attains the fruit of both. (5.4)

Śrīdhara: Since, in this way, there is a sequential combination of both [Sāṅkhya and Yoga] as primary and subordinate according to their different states, therefore, to accept an option between them and ask which of the two is superior is appropriate only for the ignorant, not for the discerning;
thus he says, "Sāṅkhya and Yoga."

By the word *sāṅkhya*, which denotes steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*), he indicates its constituent part, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). Only the ignorant, not the wise, declare that renunciation and karma-yoga—which have a single fruit—are separate and independent. The reason for this is that by properly adhering to even one of these two, one attains the fruit of both.

For thus, one who properly practices Karma-yoga becomes pure in heart and, through the door of knowledge, attains that which is the fruit of both—namely, liberation (kaivalya). Likewise, even one who is properly established in Sannyāsa attains, through the door of knowledge and by way of a succession [of stages], that which is the fruit of both—namely, liberation—even from Karma-yoga previously practiced. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no difference in the fruit of these two. //4//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might ask, how can it be understood that one who is engaged in action is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), given the essential contradiction between the nature of action and its abandonment? If you argue that this is so because their fruits are identical, we say no; for even if the fruits were identical, there would still be a logical necessity for a contradiction between two things that are essentially opposed.
Anticipating the objection that it is therefore untenable for both to be the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), he says: "Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Sāṃkhya is renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), so called because it carries (*vahati*) *saṃkhyā*—that is, right knowledge of the Self—as an internal means to wisdom.
Yoga is the previously mentioned yoga of action (*karma-yoga*).
Fools— who are devoid of the knowledge that discriminates the meaning of the scriptures— proclaim those two to have distinct and contradictory results, but the wise do not.
What, then, is the opinion of the wise?

It is said: even though there is a distinction between renunciation and action, one who is properly established in either—having performed it correctly according to the scriptures in accordance with his own qualification—obtains the fruit of both; namely, the single goal of supreme beatitude (niḥśreyasa) through the means of the arising of knowledge. //4//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, even what you have stated—that "of these two, that alone is better"—does not actually hold true; for it has been observed by the discerning that there is no distinction between the two. Thus he says: "Sāṃkhya and Yoga... [and so forth].
By the word *sāṃkhya*, which denotes steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*), its constituent part, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), is indicated.
The ignorant say that renunciation and karma-yoga are separate and independent, but not the wise, because of what was stated previously: "He should be known as one who is eternally renounced."
Therefore, [the text says] "even one," and so forth. //4//
Baladeva: He says "sāṃkhya" etc., because your statement that "one of these two is better" is also not tenable.
The ignorant, but not the wise, proclaim that the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action are distinct due to a difference in their fruits.
Therefore, the fruit characterized by the vision of the Self is "one," and so forth. //4//
The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the practitioners of Yoga. He truly sees who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one. //5//
Śrīdhara clarifies this very point with the words "by the Sāṃkhyas.
That state called liberation which is attained preeminently and directly by the Sāṃkhyas—those renunciants established in knowledge—is [attained] by the Yogins;
here, the suffix *ac* should be understood as having the sense of the matup-affix (*matvarthīya*), according to the rule for the *ārṣa* class.
Therefore, even by those who practice through action (*karma-yogin*), that very same goal is reached and attained by means of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Hence, he alone sees correctly who perceives Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, because they have a single fruit. //5//
Madhusūdana:

[The Lord] explains how one obtains the fruit of both through the performance of only one by saying, "That which [is attained] by the Sāṅkhyas," etc. By the Sāṅkhyas—those renunciants established in knowledge—even though they are devoid of the performance of actions in this life, [the goal is attained] through the actions of previous births.

Thus, by those whose internal organs are purified through steadfastness in knowledge preceded by hearing and other means, that which is known as liberation— which is established in the sense that one abides in this very state and never falls away from it— is attained; it is as if obtained merely through the removal of veils, since it is eternally present.
Even by those who possess yoga— meaning those for whom there exist scriptural actions performed with the intellect dedicated to the Blessed One and devoid of expectation for results—
the word *yoga* here being formed with the suffix *ac* in the sense of possession according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*—

even by such yogis, through the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and the practice of hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, and through steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) existing or yet to come in a future birth, that [liberation] will be attained.
A state is attained.
Therefore, because they have a single fruit, he alone who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one sees correctly, and no other.

The meaning is this: for those in whom steadfastness in knowledge preceded by renunciation is observed, that very sign leads one to infer their steadfastness in action dedicated to the Lord in previous births;
for an effect cannot arise without a cause. As it has been said:
"In other births than these, it must surely have been performed."

"What must be done by a person here [in this world] is such that there is no other way to abide in Brahman. Thus, for those in whom devotion to actions dedicated to the Lord is observed, their future steadfastness in knowledge preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is inferred by that very sign, because the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is never without its effect.
Therefore, for an ignorant seeker of liberation, the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) should first be practiced for the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), but not renunciation.
But that will occur spontaneously when there is intensity of dispassion. //5//
Viśvanātha clarifies this very point with the words "yad" (that which):
"By the Sāṃkhyas through renunciation, and by the Yogins through desireless action."
The plural number is used out of respect;
therefore, he who perceives those two as one and the same through discernment, even though they are distinct, he truly sees—he is the one with vision, the wise man—this is the meaning. //5//
Baladeva explains this with the words "yad" (that which):
by the Sāṃkhyas, who are practitioners of the yoga of knowledge, and by the Yogas, who are those of desireless action; [the suffix] *ac* is applied here according to the rule beginning with *arśas*.
The "state" (sthāna) has the characteristic of self-perception.
Therefore, although these two are of different forms by way of being cessation and engagement, he who sees—that is, knows—their oneness due to the unity of their fruit, he truly sees;
he is the one with vision, the wise man—this is the meaning. //5//
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga; the sage disciplined in yoga reaches Brahman before long. (5.6)

Śrīdhara: To one who thinks that if even those engaged in *karma-yoga* must ultimately reach steadfastness in knowledge through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) alone, then it would be more appropriate to practice renunciation from the very beginning, he says: "Renunciation.
Without yoga—that is, without *karma-yoga*—renunciation is difficult to attain; it is a cause of suffering.
The meaning is that it is impossible;
for, in the absence of purity of mind, the culmination of knowledge cannot occur.
However, the sage who is disciplined in yoga, by virtue of his pure mind, becomes a renunciant and attains Brahman very quickly indeed.
One knows [the truth] directly.
Therefore, it is established that what was stated previously—that prior to the purification of the mind, karma-yoga alone is superior to renunciation—is indeed proven.
This has been said by the authors of the Vārttika:
"Even those who have renounced the world are seen to be negligent, with minds turned outward, backbiting, and eager for quarrels, their very foundations corrupted by fate. (6)
Madhusūdana:

If it is asked, "Why should renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) not be performed first even by one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is impure, since it is necessary as the cause for steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*)?", he says in response: "Renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*).

That renunciation which is performed by force alone—without the practice of yoga, that is, without the scriptural action (*śāstrīya karma*) that purifies the internal organ—is only for the sake of attaining suffering.
Because the fruit of that [knowledge], which is steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*), is impossible for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is impure;
and because there is no qualification for action (*karman*) which purifies, one falls away from both action and Brahman, thereby encountering a supreme crisis.

However, one who is engaged in *karma-yoga* becomes a sage (*muni*)—one whose nature is reflection—and, having become a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) due to the purity of the internal organ, [attains] Brahman.
One attains—that is, directly realizes—the Self characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth, very soon, that is, quickly, because of the absence of obstacles.
And this has already been stated before:
"A person does not attain freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) through the non-commencement of actions."
"And one does not attain perfection through renunciation alone" (Gītā 3.4).

Therefore, even though they share a single fruit, it is logical that what was stated previously—that the yoga of action (karma-yoga) is superior to the renunciation of action (karma-saṃnyāsa)—is established. //6//
Viśvanātha:

However, for the knower who has not yet determined perfect purity of mind, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is painful while Karma-yoga is indeed pleasant; thus he states clearly the meaning previously indicated in the verse beginning with "But renunciation... (saṃnyāsas tu).

The phrase "when there is a deficiency of the mind" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Due to non-application" means due to the absence of the yoga of action; that is to say, because the yoga of action which pacifies the deficiencies of the mind is absent in a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), he lacks the qualification for it. Thus, renunciation leads only to suffering.

Thus it has been said by the authors of the Vārttika: "Even those who have renounced the world are seen to be negligent, with minds directed outward, malicious, and eager for quarrels, their very foundations corrupted by fate."
The Śruti also says: "If ascetics do not uproot the tangles of desire from their hearts.
The Blessed Lord has likewise said: "He who has not restrained the sixfold group [of senses]" (BhP 11.18.40), and so forth.
Therefore, a sage who is disciplined in yoga, who performs actions without desire, and who possesses knowledge, quickly attains Brahman. //6//
Baladeva: Because the yoga of knowledge is difficult to perform, He says, "But renunciation... and so forth, to show that the easily performed yoga of action is superior.
Renunciation is the yoga of knowledge, consisting of the withdrawal of the activities of all the senses;
without yoga—that is, without the yoga of action—it becomes difficult to attain [liberation].
The meaning is that [action] would indeed be a cause of suffering because it is difficult to perform and because it involves negligence.
However, the sage who performs action without desire while disciplined in yoga, being one whose nature is to contemplate the Self, attains Brahman very quickly, without delay. //6//

One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the mind and conquered the senses, and whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, such a person is not tainted. (5.7)

Śrīdhara: Anticipating the objection that even when Brahman is attained through the sequence beginning with karma-yoga, bondage might still occur due to subsequent action, he says, "one who is disciplined in yoga" (yoga-yukta).
He is one who is joined with yoga;
for this very reason, his self—that is, his mind—is purified.
Therefore, he by whom the self—that is, the body—is conquered;
therefore, he by whom the senses are conquered;
and thus, he whose self has become the self of all beings—even while performing action, whether it be for the sake of maintaining the world or as his own natural disposition—is not tainted. //7//
Madhusūdana:
Now, since action is a cause of bondage, it might be argued that the statement "the sage disciplined in yoga attains Brahman" is untenable; therefore, he says, "disciplined in yoga.
Action prescribed by the scriptures when endowed with qualities such as the absence of desire for fruits through dedication to the Blessed Lord is called "yoga."
A person endowed with that yoga first becomes one whose self is purified—that is, one whose inner faculty (*sattva*), which constitutes the self, is pure and untainted by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Being thus possessed of a stainless internal organ, he becomes one who has conquered the self, having brought his body under his own control;
thereafter, he becomes one who has conquered the senses, having brought all external organs under his own control.
By this, the *tridaṇḍin* mentioned by Manu has been explained:
"Control of speech, control of mind, and likewise control of body—he whose restraints are constant is called a *tridaṇḍin*. Thus it is said.
The word "speech" (*vāk*) is an illustration for the external sense organs.
He states that such a person necessarily attains knowledge of reality: "one whose self has become the self of all beings and whose self has become all beings.
This means one who perceives everything, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient, as being nothing but the Self alone.

If one were to explain [the compound] as "one whose self has become the self of all beings," then the word *ātmabhūta* would be redundant, since the intended meaning is already obtained by the term *sarvabhūtātman* alone.
However, it is consistent if the two terms *sarva* and *ātman* refer respectively to the insentient and the sentient.

The meaning is this: such a seer of ultimate reality, even while performing actions from the perspective of others (*para-dṛṣṭyā*), is not tainted by those actions because, from his own perspective (*sva-dṛṣṭyā*), they do not exist. //7//
Viśvanātha:
He states that even by performing action, the man of knowledge (jñānin) incurs no taint: "One who is disciplined in yoga...

The man of knowledge disciplined in yoga is of three kinds: one whose self is purified and who has conquered his intellect; [the other two are]... [one whose doubts have been destroyed and who is established in wisdom].
The second is one who has conquered the self and possesses a purified mind;
the third is one who has conquered the sense faculties.
There is an increase in excellence due to the progressive refinement of the means employed by each preceding stage.
He states that all living beings indeed take delight in such a householder: he is one whose very self—his body—is the beloved object of affection for all beings. (7)
Baladeva: He says "yoga" etc., meaning that such a seeker of liberation is dear to all. "Yoked" (yukta) means devoted to yoga, which is desireless action;
for this very reason, he is "pure-souled," meaning one whose intellect is stainless.
Therefore, he is one who has conquered the self, having brought the mind under control;
therefore, he is one who has mastered the senses, being free from attachment to objects such as sound;
and therefore, he is one whose self—his body—is the very self of all beings and living creatures, having become the object of their love.

Nor is identity with the Self of all intended here by the Charioteer of Pārtha—since he declares the mutual difference between all selves in the passage beginning with "But I am not," and because even one who asserts such [identity] would be unable to speak of the difference between the enlightened and the ignorant.
One who is thus situated, though acting, is not tainted by the conceit of self in what is not-self due to the contemplation of the distinct Self; he attains the Self before long.
Therefore, the yoga of action is superior. //7//
"Even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing, the disciplined knower of truth should think: 'I do nothing at all. (5.8)
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening the eyes, or even closing them—he should maintain the awareness that it is merely the senses operating upon their respective objects. //9//

Śrīdhara: Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory to say "even while performing action, one is not tainted," he states with two verses, beginning with "not indeed," that there is no contradiction because of the absence of the conceit of agency.

One who is disciplined in *karma-yoga*, having gradually become a knower of reality, even while performing seeing, hearing, and so forth, maintains—determining through his intellect—that "the senses are merely operating upon their objects," and thus thinks, "I do nothing at all. He reflects in this manner.
In this context, seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating are the functions of the cognitive faculties (jñānendriya) such as the eye and so forth; walking is the function of the feet;
and sleeping is the function of the intellect (buddhi).
Breathing is the function of the organ of life; speech is that of the organ of speech;
and evacuation is that of the anus and the generative organ.
"Seizing" refers to the two hands;
"opening and closing" refers to the vital breath known as Kūrma—this is the distinction.
Even while performing these actions, the knower of Brahman is not tainted due to the absence of egoistic identification.
And likewise, the *Parāmarṣa-sūtra* states: "Upon the attainment of that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof. (8–9)
Madhusūdana explains this very point with two verses beginning with "naiva":
[He is not perceived] by the organs of knowledge such as the eyes, nor by the organs of action such as speech, nor by the various vital airs such as prāṇa, nor by the fourfold internal organ.
And while those various activities are being performed, the senses—the sense organs and so forth—alone operate and function with respect to their respective objects, their own specific domains;
yet, maintaining and discerning "I am not," the knower of reality, the seer of the supreme truth, being disciplined and concentrated in mind, thinks, "I do nothing at all. He reflects thus.

Alternatively, the connection is as follows: first one is engaged through the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*), and subsequently, by means of the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*), having become a knower of reality (*tattvavit*), one thinks, "I do nothing at all.

In that context, seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating are stated to be the functions of the five organs of knowledge—the eyes, ears, skin, nose, and tongue—expressed as "seeing," "hearing," "touching," "smelling," and "eating."
Movement belongs to the feet;
idle chatter to speech;
and emission to the anus and genitals.

"Grasping with the hands" refers to the five functions of the organs of action, which are described as going, speaking, releasing, grasping, and so forth. "Breathing" is an indicative mark for the function of the pentad beginning with *prāṇa*. "Opening and closing the eyes" indicates the function of the pentad beginning with *nāga* and *kūrma*.
The phrase "while sleeping" refers to the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
These two verses have been explained by breaking the order of the text in accordance with the sequence of their meaning;
for [the yogi] perceives that the Self is indeed a non-agent even amidst all activities.
Therefore, the sense is that it is indeed rightly said, "even while acting, he is not tainted. //8-9//
Viśvanātha:
He does not teach that one should engage in such action as would lead to attachment.

A disciplined practitioner of *karma-yoga*, even while performing seeing and other such acts, maintains and resolves through his intellect that "the senses are merely operating upon their objects," remaining free from egoism and thinking, "I am not doing anything at all."
He thinks thus. //8-9//
Baladeva: He teaches that for the pure Self, there is no agency with respect to action that requires the five factors such as the locus (adhiṣṭhāna) and so forth, by the words "not at all" (naiva).

One who is disciplined—a performer of desireless action—even while performing actions such as seeing due to contact with the body, senses, and other elements which are composed of the primary qualities (pradhāna), is a knower of reality; experiencing the distinct reality of the Self, he withdraws his senses—the eyes and so forth—from the objects of the senses, such as forms and the like.
Maintaining and ascertaining that "these [actions] proceed impelled by the Supreme Self in accordance with my own latent impressions (vāsanā)," one considers that "I do nothing at all.

In the phrase "seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating," the activities of seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating belong to the organs of knowledge— the eyes, ears, skin, nose, and tongue.
In that context, movement pertains to the feet; incoherent speech to the tongue;
and the bliss of emission to the anus and the generative organ.
It should be understood that "grasping" refers to the two hands;

"breathing" refers to the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth; "opening and closing [the eyes]" refers to the various types of vital breaths such as Nāga and the rest; and "sleeping" refers to the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa).
This is the meaning; it should be explained in sequence as follows:

"The sense is that for me, whose singular essence is consciousness and bliss, this agency regarding such actions is caused by the connection with the body and so forth—which is dominated by beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā)—and not caused by my own essential nature. This is the intended meaning.
It cannot be asserted that the self’s agency is not in any way inherent to its own nature, because it is designated as such in relation to both determination and reflection;
moreover, that [agency] is indeed knowledge, and that is eternal for the self, for the scripture states: "For the knower, there is no loss of the act of knowing."
And they say that its accomplishment is through Hari, who has become Dharma, and through knowledge. //8-9//
He who performs actions by placing them in Brahman and abandoning attachment is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (5.10)
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, for one who possesses the conceit 'I am doing this,' the taint of action is unavoidable;

and because his mind is thus impure, even renunciation (saṃnyāsa) does not exist—thus a great dilemma has arisen. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In Brahman" (brahmaṇi), meaning having offered or surrendered to the Supreme Lord.

And having abandoned attachment to the fruit thereof, he who performs actions is not tainted by that action— which, being the cause of bondage, is most sinful and consists of both merit and demerit— just as a lotus leaf, though situated in water, is not tainted by that water. //10//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: In that case, the ignorant person would surely be tainted by the conceit of agency; and if so, how could he attain steadfastness in knowledge preceded by renunciation? To this, He says: "In Brahman... Having placed—that is, having surrendered—their actions in Brahman, the Supreme Lord, and having abandoned attachment, which is the desire for results, they act for the sake of the Lord like servants.

He who performs worldly and Vedic actions with the intention, "I act for the sake of the Master (the Lord), being indifferent to my own fruit," is not smeared by evil— that is to say, by action consisting of both merit and demerit—
just as a lotus leaf is not smeared by water poured upon it.
Action performed with the intention of offering it to the Blessed One shall have the purification of the intellect as its sole fruit. //10//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, he who, having surrendered [all] to Me—the Supreme Lord, Brahman—and having abandoned attachment, performs actions even while possessing self-identity, having relinquished attachment to action;
by the word "sin," [other] defects are indicated by way of illustration.
He, too, is not defiled by mere action alone. //10//
Baladeva, clarifying what was stated, says: "In Brahman.
Here, by the word *brahman*, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) in its state of the three qualities (*guṇas*) is meant, because of the scriptural statement:
"From that [Brahman], this [world]—consisting of name, form, and food—is known."

And from the statement to be made later, "My womb is the Great Brahman," it follows that the body, senses, and so forth are specific transformations of Pradhāna; for when Pradhāna has transformed into those forms, the functions such as seeing are attributed to it alone.
The meaning is that one should determine, "These belong to that [Pradhāna] alone, and not to me, who am distinct from it and pure."
Having abandoned attachment— which is the desire for the fruits [of action]— as well as the insistence on being their agent,
he who performs those actions is not tainted by the evil of identifying with the body and so forth, even though he exists as one possessing such a body and so on;
it is just like a lotus leaf, which remains untouched even when sprinkled with water poured upon it.
And the phrase "having renounced actions unto me" should not be explained as "unto Brahman, the Supreme Self," because of the inherent force of the preceding context;

for the subject under discussion is that the agency of actions such as seeing belongs only to the individual soul (jīva) as associated with the primary elements, the body, and so forth, and not to the soul when separated from those. //10//
By means of the body, mind, intellect, and even the senses alone, yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification. (5.11)

Śrīdhara: The fruit of that action would be merely the purification of the *sattva*, because of the phrase "with the body. That is, with the body (*kāya*), which is the physical frame, as well as with the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*). For the yogi who has abandoned attachment, even with the body, mind, and intellect—indeed, even with the sense organs alone.

The word "only" (*kevala*) is connected with each [factor], such as the body and so forth. To abandon the sense of "mine" (*mamatā*) regarding all activities, the yogi who performs action performs his work while abandoning attachment to the object of its fruit.
The meaning is "for the purification of the self" and "for the purification of the being.
Therefore, your qualification (adhikāra) lies in that very [practice] alone. //11//

Madhusūdana explains that very point with the words "by the body," etc.: yogis who are performers of action, having abandoned attachment to the fruits, perform action by means of the body, mind, intellect, and even the senses; the word "exclusively" (*kevalaiḥ*) is an adjective qualifying all these—body and so forth.
The meaning is: "I perform [this] for the Lord alone, not for the sake of my own fruit," being devoid of the sense of "mine-ness.
And "for the purification of the self" means for the purpose of purifying the mind. //11//
Viśvanātha:

"By the senses alone" means that even though at the time of offering the oblation and so forth with the mantra "svāhā to Indra" and others, the mind might be elsewhere, nevertheless [the sacrifice is still performed]. This is the meaning.
For the sake of purifying the self, for the purpose of purifying the mind. //11//
Baladeva, validating right conduct (*sad-ācāra*), explains this with the words "by the body" and so forth:
yogis perform actions accomplished by means of the body and other instruments while being devoid of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) regarding the body and so on;
[they act] solely with pure [instruments].
"Having abandoned attachment," as before, for the sake of self-purification—that is, for the cessation of the beginningless identification of the body with the self. //11//
The disciplined one, having renounced the fruit of action, attains peace that is final; the undisciplined one, through acting out of desire, becomes bound by attachment to the fruit. 12.
Śrīdhara: Now, how is it that by the very same action one is liberated while another is bound?
To this he says: "the disciplined one" (yuktaḥ).
Being disciplined—meaning being solely devoted to the Supreme Lord—one who performs action having renounced the fruit of action attains ultimate peace, which is liberation.
But the unyoked one, being outward-turned, through acting according to his own will and desire, and being attached to the fruits of action, attains extreme bondage. //12//
Madhusūdana:

Even though the sense of agency (*kartṛtva-abhimāna*) is the same for both, what is the cause of this discrepancy—that by that very same action one is liberated while another is bound? To this he says: "The disciplined one" (*yukta*). One who is disciplined is one whose intention is such that "these actions are for the sake of the Lord alone, not for my own fruit," having thus renounced the fruit of action.

Performing actions, one attains the peace known as liberation— that is to say, the peace born through the sequence of purification of the mind, discrimination of the eternal reality, renunciation, and steadfastness in knowledge.

On the other hand, he who is undisciplined, devoid of the intention that "these actions are for the Lord alone and not for my own fruit," being attached to the fruit through acting according to desire— acting out of personal whim with the thought "I perform this action for my own fruit"— is bound.
One attains a firm bondage to saṃsāra through actions;
since this is so, the completion of the sentence is: "Therefore, you too, being disciplined, should perform actions. //12//
Viśvanātha:

He states that non-attachment and attachment while performing action are themselves the causes of liberation and bondage; the meaning is that the "disciplined yogi" is one who performs action without desire.
"Ultimate peace" means liberation attained through steadfastness (*naiṣṭhikīm* = *niṣṭhā-prāptām*).
The meaning is that he is unrighteous, being an agent of action driven by desire; [this occurs] through acting according to desire, that is, through the engagement in desire. //12//

Baladeva: One whose mind is disciplined and surrendered, having renounced the fruit of action, attains the steadfast peace characterized by the vision of the Self through performing [action] with constancy. One whose mind is undisciplined and not surrendered, being attached to the fruit of action, is bound by acting according to desire—that is, by engaging in action out of personal whim—and thus transmigrates. //12//
Renouncing all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied being dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action to be done. (5.13)

Śrīdhara: Thus far, it has been elaborated that for one whose mind is devoid of purity, Karma-yoga is superior to renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Now, he says "all actions" (sarva-karmāṇi) to show that for one of pure mind, renunciation is superior.
"The self-controlled" (vaśī) means one whose mind is restrained.

Having renounced all distracting activities with a mind endowed with discernment, he remains established in knowledge so that there may be happiness. Where does he remain? To this he says: "in the nine gates.
These are the two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the mouth—these seven located in the head.
The two located below are the forms of the anus and the genitals.

Thus, in that city which possesses nine gates—that body which is empty of ego (ahaṃkāra)—the embodied one (dehin) dwells. Precisely because of the absence of ego, he does not act with that body himself; and because of the absence of the sense of "mine" (mama-kāra), he does not cause others to act. In this way, the turning away from the impure mind is described.
For one whose mind is impure, having renounced, acts again or causes others to act;
but this one is not like that.
The meaning is that he dwells in inner happiness. //13//
Madhusūdana:

Having elaborated upon the previously stated point that for one of impure mind, Karma-yoga is superior to mere renunciation (saṃnyāsa), he now says that for one of pure mind, the renunciation of all actions alone is superior:
"All actions—whether obligatory, occasional, optional, or prohibited—one should perceive as non-action through the mind while performing action."

Having renounced—that is, having completely abandoned—by means of the right vision of the nature of the Self as a non-agent, which was mentioned in the verse beginning with "he who should see," he remains or stays exactly as he is through the force of *prārabdha* karma.
To the question "Is there suffering?", he says "no"; he remains in happiness, without effort, because he is devoid of the activities of body, speech, and mind that cause exertion.

"Why do the body, speech, and mind not act according to their own will? To this he says: "The Master," one who has brought under his own control the aggregate of the instruments (the organs) that perform their functions. Where does he abide? "In the city of nine gates": two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, and the voice as one—these seven in the head;
and two known as the anus and the generative organ below—thus in the body distinguished by these nine gates.

The embodied one (dehin), who perceives the Self as distinct from the body, remains like a traveler in another's house, neither rejoicing nor desponding over honors or insults directed toward that [body], being devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine.
For the ignorant person, due to the conceit of identifying with the body, is merely the body and not the embodied one.
And he, regarding the body as the very locus of the Self, identifies "I was in the house" or "I was on the ground," but not "I was in the body," because of his lack of perception of difference.
However, one who perceives the Self as distinct from the aggregate [of the body and organs] and has renounced all actions, through the perception of difference, realizes "I was in the body.

Therefore, the renunciation of all actions is said to be precisely the sublation by knowledge (*vidyā*) of those activities of the body and so forth which have been superimposed upon the actionless Self through ignorance (*avidyā*).
For this very reason, to distinguish [the Self] from the ignorant, it is said that He "dwells in the city with nine gates.

Now, one might object: even if the activities of the body and so forth—which are superimposed upon the Self—are sublated by knowledge, just as the movement of a boat is [seen not in] the tree standing on the bank, the Self would still possess agency through its own activity and the status of a director regarding the activities of the body and so forth.
"No," he says; the connection is that one "remains" neither acting nor causing others to act. //13//
Viśvanātha:

Therefore, even while performing actions without attachment, he should be known as a "constant renunciant" (*nitya-saṃnyāsī*); as stated previously, in reality, he is indeed called a renunciant. Regarding this, [the Lord] says: having mentally renounced all actions, yet performing them externally through the activity of the body and so forth.
Moreover, the self-controlled one who has conquered his senses dwells in happiness.

Where? In the city of nine gates—the body which is devoid of the sense of "I"—the embodied soul, having attained knowledge, dwells knowing that, in reality, there is no agency in the pleasure derived from action, thinking "I am not the doer," nor is there even the agency of instigation, thinking "I am not the one causing others to act. This is the meaning. //13//
Baladeva: Regarding the word "all":

with a mind characterized by discrimination (*viveka*), having renounced—that is, surrendered—all actions to such a Primal Nature (*pradhāna*), the self-controlled one—meaning one who has conquered the senses—remains at ease even while performing them externally through the body and other instruments.
In the city of nine gates—in the body, which is like a city and devoid of the sense of "I"—there are two eyes, two nostrils, two ears, and the mouth.
And on the head there are seven openings, while below there are two known as the anus and the genitals; thus, the embodied soul who has attained knowledge [perceives] these nine doors.
"Not at all" means that he understands that for the Self, which is distinct from the body and so forth, there is neither agency nor causality in actions. //13//
The Lord creates neither the agency nor the actions of the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is inherent nature that operates. 14.

Śrīdhara: But surely, according to such scriptural passages as, "For it is He alone who causes him to perform good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; He causes him to perform evil action whom He wishes to lead downward," the person is not independent, being impelled by the Supreme Lord Himself as the agent in actions that yield auspicious or inauspicious fruits;
how then could he renounce those actions?
If it is argued that "one who is directed by the Lord alone upon the path of knowledge will abandon both the auspicious and the inauspicious," then,

fearing that the Lord would likewise incur a connection with merit and sin because He is the instigating agent through His partiality and cruelty, he says [the following] in two verses beginning with "not agency":
"The Lord, the Sovereign, does not create the agency and so forth of the world of living beings."
However, it is the very nature of the individual soul (jīva) that ignorance manifests itself in the form of agency and so forth.
By the power of beginningless ignorance and desire, the Lord impels the world of living beings—whose nature is to act—to engage in actions;
the meaning is that He does not Himself produce agency and the like. //14//
Madhusūdana:

Just as the movement inherent in Devadatta does not exist when his state of rest is present, so too the agency and causality of the Self do not exist as inherent properties when there is true renunciation (*sannyāsa*).

Alternatively, since they do not exist there by way of the actual nature of things—just as the surface-dirtiness and the like do not exist in the sky—he says, "There is no agency," in order to dispel doubt.

The meaning is that the Lord, the Self, the Master, does not exercise agency over the body and so forth of the world; He is not their director by means of a command such as "you must create" or "you must act.
Nor does He Himself create the objects of action—such as pots and the like—which are most desired by the world; the meaning is that He is not even their agent.
Furthermore, He does not create for the world the connection with the fruit of actions once they have been performed; the meaning is that He is neither their provider of enjoyment nor their enjoyer.

"Being equal, he does not move through both worlds; he meditates, as it were, he vibrates, as it were"—so says the Śruti. And here too it is said: "Though dwelling in the body, O Kaunteya, he neither acts nor is tainted" (Gītā 13.31). If the Self by its own nature neither causes anything to be done nor acts itself, then who is it that, causing and acting, engages in activity? To this, he replies: "But it is nature... (svabhāvas tu...).
Divine Māyā, whose nature is ignorance, functions as Prakṛti. //14//
Viśvanātha:

Now, if the individual soul (jīva) does not possess agency and so forth in reality, then since we observe the soul’s agency, enjoyership, and so on everywhere in this world created by the Supreme Lord, I think that the Supreme Lord himself must have forcibly created its agency and other such qualities.
That being the case, since the faults of partiality and cruelty would follow,
he says "no" to that— namely, "there is no agency"—
and also, by virtue of such agency, there are no actions either.
Nor is there even a conjunction with the enjoyments that are the fruits of karma;
rather, it is the very nature of the individual soul (jīva)—namely, beginningless ignorance—that proceeds.
The sense is that this ignorance functions in order to cause that soul to ascend to the conceit of agency and so forth. //14//
Baladeva: He clarifies that these two do not exist for the pure [Self] with the word "no.

The Lord—the master of the body, senses, and so forth—is the individual soul (*jīva*); he does not create the agency of the world or of people, meaning he is not one who causes others to act by saying, "You do it.
Nor does he create the objects most desired by that [soul], such as garlands, garments, and the like; thus, he is not even the agent himself.

The meaning is that it does not create—nor bring about the conjunction or connection with—the fruit of action, whether pleasure or pain; thus, it is neither the one who causes others to experience nor the experiencer itself.
If this is so, then who is perceived as the one who causes and the one who acts?
To this, he says: "But [it is] inherent nature (svabhāva)."

The primary latent impression (*pradhāna-vāsanā*), which has functioned since beginningless time, is here designated by the term "nature" (*svabhāva*). The individual soul (*jīva*), possessing a body and so forth produced by that nature, is the instigator and the agent; thus, the reality is not distinct [from it].

Even in the pure [state], there is indeed a certain degree of agency, because of what was stated previously regarding the reality in the context of the "easy seat" (*sukhāsana*); this should be understood as being like [the case of] appearance and so forth.
For action (*kriyā*) is indeed the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
For agency has been stated to be the primary state of that [self]. //14//
The all-pervading Lord does not take on the sin or even the merit of anyone;
knowledge is enveloped by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded. (15)
Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore [the Lord] "does not take" (nādatta).
Even though He is the instigator and the master, He does not at all take—that is, He does not partake of—the sin or the merit of anyone.
The reason for this is: He is the all-pervading (vibhu), that is, perfectly complete.
The meaning is "one whose desires are fulfilled.
For if he were to cause [others] to act out of a desire for his own self-interest, then it would be so;
but this is not the case.
Because He, whose desires are already fulfilled, acts as the impeller of various things according to their respective prior karma through His own inconceivable *māyā*.
[Objection: "But since partiality is observed in Him—bestowing grace upon devotees while inflicting punishment upon non-devotees—how can it be said that His desires are fulfilled?
To this, he says: "By ignorance."
Even punishment in the form of a rod is indeed a form of grace;
thus, the knowledge that the Supreme Lord is equal toward all, even in ignorance, is obscured. For that reason, living beings—sentient creatures—are deluded.
The meaning is that they consider there to be partiality in the Blessed One. //15//
Madhusūdana:
But surely the Lord is the cause of action and the individual soul (jīva) is the agent;
for thus says the Śruti: "He indeed makes him whom He wishes to lead upward perform good deeds."
"This very [Self] indeed causes him to perform evil action whom He wishes to lead downward," and so forth; and also the Smṛti:
"This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or even to hell."

And thus, since the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) would respectively incur the taint of sin and merit through their states of being the agent and the instigator, or the enjoyer and the one who causes enjoyment, how can it be said that "nature alone proceeds"? To this he replies: "He does not take.

In the ultimate sense, the all-pervading Supreme Lord does not at all take upon Himself the sin or the good deed of any individual soul; for in the ultimate sense, the individual soul lacks agency, and the Supreme Lord lacks the status of an instigator.

How then are the Śruti, Smṛti, and worldly convention [to be understood]? To this he says: Knowledge—which is the substratum for the delusion of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and the world; which is eternal, self-luminous, of the nature of existence-consciousness-bliss (sac-cid-ānanda), non-dual, and the ultimate reality—is covered and concealed by ignorance (ajñāna), known as Māyā, which possesses the powers of veiling (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa), and is unreal (anṛta). This is the darkness (tamas) that obscures it.

Due to that obscuration of one's true nature (*svarūpāvaraṇa*), living beings—those characterized by repeated birth, wandering in *saṃsāra*, and failing to perceive the true nature of reality—become deluded. They fall into a ninefold delusion consisting of the subject, the object, the means of knowledge, the agent, the action, the instrument, the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment; that is, they undergo the distraction (*vikṣepa*) which consists in the appearance of something as what it is not.

This perceived delusion of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and the world exists among the ignorant, being rooted in the failure to perceive the nature of the Self, which is a non-agent, a non-enjoyer, supreme bliss, and non-dual.
And in that state, these two Śruti and Smṛti texts, which conform to the cognition of the deluded, are subsidiary to the statements that awaken one to real non-duality; thus there is no fault. //15//
Viśvanātha: Since the Lord is not the one who causes those of evil and good deeds to act, for that very reason He does not share in their sin or merit; thus he says, "He does not take."
It does not take or grasp;

rather, it is indeed that power of his which is ignorance (avidyā) that veils the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva). Thus he says: "by ignorance," meaning by avidyā. Knowledge is the innate nature of the individual soul.
For that reason. //15//

Baladeva: Now, if you say that the pure individual soul (jīva) lacks such agency regarding karma and so forth, then it follows—by the force of curiosity—that the Supreme Self (paramātman), having cast the primary matter (pradhāna) around its neck, fashioned for it the body, senses, and so on, which are the transformations of that [matter].
And this is logical.

Otherwise, there is the Śruti: "For it is He indeed who causes him whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds to perform good deeds; and it is He indeed who causes him whom He wishes to lead down to perform evil deeds.
[And: "This living being is ignorant and not master of its own pleasure and pain."
Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even to the sky.
Otherwise, the traditional teaching (smṛti) would be contradicted;
and thus it would lead to a state consisting of sin and merit.
If it is argued that the instigator would consequently incur inequality and so forth, as well as a share in the sin and other consequences, he says in response: "it is not taken."

The Lord—the Supreme Self—is all-pervading, consisting of immeasurable consciousness and bliss, full of infinite power, whose sole essence is His own bliss, and who is indifferent toward anything other than Himself.

He causes the individual soul (*jīva*)—who is bound by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless primordial matter (*pradhāna*), who desires enjoyment, and who possesses a body and so forth produced from *pradhāna* through His mere proximity—to perform actions according to those very impressions. Yet, He does not take upon Himself, nor does He seize, the sins or the merits of any individual soul.
Thus it is stated in the Śrī-Vaiṣṇava:
"Just as fragrance causes agitation of the mind by its mere presence, and not because it performs any service, so too is that Supreme Lord."
"Just as space, time, and so forth are causes of a tree by virtue of their mere proximity,
in the very same way, the Blessed Lord Hari is the cause of the universe through non-transformation.
In this regard, this example of fragrance and so forth refers only to [the Lord's] state of indifference (*audāsīnya*), and not to the absence of His will (*icchā*).
Because it is heard in scripture that "he desired";
if so, why do the living beings speak of him as being unequal?
To this he says: "through ignorance."
By means of beginningless ignorance that is averse to That, the eternal knowledge of living beings is covered and concealed.
For that reason, creatures—that is, individual souls—become deluded;
the meaning is that, though it is equal, the deluded call it unequal, whereas the wise do not.
And the author of the Sūtras says thus: "Inequality and cruelty [on the part of God] do not follow, because He has regard [for karma]; for so He shows [in scripture].
If it be argued that there is no such thing as karma because there was no differentiation [before creation], we say no, because [the cycle of existence] is beginningless. (VS 2.1.35–36) //15//
But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge, that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun. 16.
Śrīdhara: He says "by knowledge" to show that the wise do not delude themselves.

For those whose ignorance—which perceives inequality in the Blessed One—has been destroyed by the knowledge of the Lord, that knowledge, having destroyed their ignorance, reveals that supreme, perfect nature of the Lord;
just as the sun, having dispelled darkness, reveals the entire multitude of objects, so it is in this case. //16//
Madhusūdana:
In that case, since all are veiled by ignorance (ajñāna) from the beginningless [time], how could there be a cessation of saṃsāra?
To this he says: "By knowledge" (jñānena).

That ignorance—which is the root of the wind of misfortune, consisting of an indefinable falsehood such as the power of obscuration, distraction, and intoxication; which is called by terms such as *avidyā* and *māyā*; and which has the Self as both its locus and its object—is [destroyed] by the non-conceptual direct realization (*nirvikalpaka-sākṣātkāra*) of the Self, which takes the form of a modification of the internal organ purified by the maturation of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption, and is produced by the great Vedāntic statements (*mahāvākya*) taught by the Guru through knowledge.

For those who have perfected the means of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*), that which has been destroyed and sublated by a cognition whose object is solely the reality consisting of the single, indivisible essence of pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss— the non-difference between the purified meanings of *tat* and *tvam*— is known through its unreality to be non-existent even in the three periods of time, and is reduced to the state of the underlying consciousness alone, just as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is [sublated] by the knowledge of the shell.
For those seekers of liberation who have been graced by the Blessed One, that knowledge acts as follows: just as the sun,
by its mere rising, dispels darkness entirely without requiring any assistance whatsoever,
so too the knowledge of Brahman— being a transformation of pure *sattva*— is of the nature of all-pervading light.

By its very arising, without depending on any other auxiliary cause, it removes ignorance along with its effects; it reveals the single, non-dual supreme reality of the Self, whose nature is true being, consciousness, and infinite bliss, manifesting it by mere reflection without the status of an object.

Here, by stating that ignorance is "covered" and "destroyed" by knowledge, its nature as a mere absence of knowledge is excluded through its characteristics of being an obscuration and being destructible by knowledge.
For an absence does not obscure anything, nor is the absence of knowledge destroyed by knowledge, since its very nature is destruction.

Therefore, it is the Blessed One’s view that ignorance is indeed a positive entity (bhāva-rūpa), established by the direct perception of the witness-consciousness (sākṣi-pratyakṣa) in such experiences as "I am ignorant" and "I do not know myself or another."
The detailed exposition, however, is to be seen in the *Advaitasiddhi*.
By the use of the plural "of whom" (*yeṣām*), it is shown that there is no restriction [to specific individuals].
And thus says the Śruti: "Of the gods, whoever awakened to That, he indeed became That; and so it was with the seers."

Likewise, regarding humans, even now there is the passage beginning with, "He who knows thus— 'I am Brahman'— he becomes all this," and so forth; this demonstrates the absence of restriction as established by logic, namely that the cessation of ignorance— which has a particular object and a particular locus— occurs through the valid knowledge (pramāṇa-jñāna) that has that same object and that same locus.
In that regard, the obscuration pertaining to ignorance is of two kinds: one which renders existent things non-existent, and another which renders manifest things unmanifest.
Among these, the former is removed by mere valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) alone, whether it be mediate (*parokṣa*) or immediate (*aparokṣa*);
for even when fire and so forth have been inferred on a mountain, one does not observe such delusions as "there is no fire on the mountain."
Similarly, although there is a mediate certainty from the statement "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," the delusion that "Brahman does not exist" is indeed removed.
There are two factors that produce delusion: first, [the thought] "Brahman certainly exists, but it does not appear to me"; second, the obscuration of non-appearance (*abhānāvaraṇa*).
It is only through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that these are removed.
And that direct realization is produced by the Vedāntic sentences alone as being non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka); this and more should be investigated in the *Advaitasiddhi*. //16//
Viśvanātha:
Just as his ignorance veils his knowledge, so too does his other power, knowledge (vidyā-śakti), destroy that ignorance and manifest knowledge; this is the meaning.

By means of knowledge—that is, by the power of wisdom—one [overcomes] ignorance, which is nescience (*avidyā*). Knowledge itself is the agent for those living beings, like the sun; just as the radiance of the sun, having destroyed darkness, illuminates jars, cloths, and other objects, so too does knowledge.
In the same way, having destroyed ignorance by means of knowledge alone, that knowledge residing in the individual soul (jīva) reveals the supreme, non-material [Self].
Therefore, the Supreme Lord binds no one,
nor does He liberate anyone.
However, ignorance and knowledge are indeed attributes of *prakṛti* alone; they respectively bind and liberate.
Agency, enjoyership, and being the instigator thereof are the bondages;
non-attachment, tranquility, and so forth are the liberators—all these being attributes of *prakṛti* alone.

However, it is only insofar as those various attributes of *prakṛti* are awakened within Him by His being the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) that He possesses the status of an instigator; thus, His partiality and cruelty do not apply.
Baladeva says "by knowledge" (*jñānena*) to show that the wise are not deluded, citing [Gītā 4.36]:
"All [is crossed over] by the raft of knowledge alone."

For those devoted to the virtuous, whose ignorance— that aversion toward the Truth— is destroyed and utterly annihilated by that knowledge concerning one's own self and the Supreme Self, which is obtained through the grace of a true guru and possesses the majesty described in such passages as "The fire of knowledge consumes all actions" (Gītā 4.37) and "Indeed, there is nothing equal to knowledge" (Gītā 4.38).
That knowledge, acting as the agent, reveals the Supreme;
it makes known the individual soul (jīva) as distinct from the body and so forth, and the Supreme Lord (Īśvara) who is beyond defects such as inequality.
Just like the sun, when the sun has risen, it dispels darkness and reveals objects exactly as they are.
Thus, self-knowledge obtained through the instruction of a true guru is the reality of the Self as it truly is.
Here, by declaring the multiplicity of individual souls (*jīvas*) whose ignorance has been destroyed, the Charioteer of Pārtha demonstrated their [apparent] plurality in liberation;

and that [plurality], which was previously stated in the opening passage "These lords of men... and was based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikatva*), has now been refuted along with its supporting arguments. //16//

With their intellects fixed on That, their selves absorbed in That, established in That, and devoted to That, they go to the state from which there is no return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge. (5.17)
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit for those who worship the Lord in such a manner with the words "tad-buddhayaḥ" (those whose intellect is fixed on Him).
Those whose intellect—consisting of certainty—is directed toward Him alone;
those whose self—that is, their mind—is fixed on Him alone.
Those whose finality and intent are fixed on that very [state]; those for whom that alone is the supreme goal and refuge;
and consequently, those by whom the impurity has been shaken off and cast away through self-knowledge obtained by His grace.
They attain liberation, from which there is no returning again. //17//
Madhusūdana:
When the reality of the Supreme Self is revealed through knowledge, they possess that as their intellect;
that is, with the external abandonment of all objects, [they remain] in that reality of the Supreme Self revealed by knowledge, which is a mass of pure existence, consciousness, and bliss.
