The meaning is that those whose intellect—the function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*)—has reached its culmination through the ripening of spiritual practice (*sādhana-paripāka*), being characterized by direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), are "those of such intellect" (*tad-buddhayaḥ*); they are always possessed of seedless meditative absorption (*nirbīja-samādhi*).

The point is this: although there exists the relationship of the knower (*boddhṛ*)—the individual soul (*jīva*)—and the object to be known (*boddhavya*)—the reality of Brahman (*brahma-tattva*), this distinction between knower and object to be known is merely a manifestation of *māyā* and does not contradict their actual non-difference (*avastava-abheda*).
But is it not the case that the qualification "having that as their self" (*tad-ātmānaḥ*) is redundant?
For a qualification of the "knowers" (*vidvats*) serves to exclude the "ignorant" (*avidvats*).
If it is argued that since even the ignorant are, in reality, "having that as their self," how can there be an exclusion of them, we say: no.
This is because the intention is to exclude [the self] from being anything other than that.
For the ignorant, who possess the conceit of "self" with respect to the body and so forth—which are not the self—are not designated as "having that as their self.

But the wise, having ceased the conceit of body and so forth, are designated as "having that as their self" through the cessation of what is contrary [to the true self]; thus, the qualification is appropriate.

Now, one might ask: "If there is distraction caused by the performance of ritual actions (*karmānuṣṭhāna*), how can the cessation of the identification with the body and so forth occur? To this, he says: "Those who are established in that" (*tan-niṣṭhāḥ*). Those whose steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*)—that is, their state of abiding—is in that very Brahman alone, through the cessation of distraction caused by the performance of all ritual actions, are "established in that.
The meaning is that, by means of the renunciation of all ritual actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*), they are solely intent upon the inquiry into That.

If there is attachment to the fruit, how can there be renunciation of the action that serves as its means? To this he says: "devoted to That" (*tat-parāyaṇāḥ*). Those for whom That alone is the supreme goal (*param ayana*), the object to be attained, are "devoted to That.
The meaning is that they are detached from everything else.
In this context, by the phrase "having that as their cognition," direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is expressed.

By the phrase "having that as their self," the investigation of the Vedānta—consisting of the ripening of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*)—is indicated, which has as its fruit the cessation of the erroneous state consisting in the conceit of a self (*anātmābhimāna*).
By the phrase "devoted to that," the excellence of dispassion (*vairāgya*) is meant. Thus, one should understand that each preceding factor serves as the cause for each subsequent one.
Ascetics endowed with the aforementioned qualifications go to the state of non-return; that is, they attain liberation, which consists in the absence of further connection with a body.
To the question, "Why should there not be a renewed connection with a body even for those who have once been liberated? he replies: "Those whose impurities have been shaken off by knowledge.
By knowledge, the impurity consisting of merit and demerit—the cause of further connection with a body—has been shaken off, meaning it has been uprooted along with its very root.
"Those for whom [karma exists] are such [as they are described].

The sense is: since karma is destroyed through knowledge by the cessation of beginningless ignorance and its effects, how could the assumption of a body—which is rooted in that [karma]—occur again? //17//
Viśvanātha:

However, knowledge reveals only the knowledge of the individual self (jīvātman), and not the knowledge of the supreme self (paramātman), according to the Lord’s statement: "I am to be attained by exclusive devotion alone."

Therefore, even for those possessed of knowledge, devotion must be practiced specifically for the sake of attaining knowledge of the Supreme Self; hence he says, "Those whose intellect is fixed on That" (*tad-buddhayaḥ*).
By the word *tat* ("That"), the all-pervading Lord previously introduced is referred to.
The meaning is: those whose intellect is directed toward that Supreme Lord alone, being intent on meditating upon Him.
The meaning is that they have Him as their self, He as their mind, and they meditate on Him alone.
They are "established in Him" (tan-niṣṭhāḥ), because of the Lord’s statement: "One should surrender knowledge unto Me.
Even though there is a sattvic knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, they abandon steadfastness in that and remain steadfast in Him alone.
Those who have that as their supreme goal are intent upon hearing and chanting about Him,
as it will be said:
"By devotion one comes to know Me in truth— how great I am and what I am."
"Then, having known Me in truth, he enters into That immediately thereafter" (Gītā 18.55).
Those whose impurities have been shaken off by knowledge, and by means of that very knowledge, have already destroyed all ignorance even beforehand. //17//
Baladeva: He states the fruit for those who meditate upon the Supreme Self as being devoid of partiality and so forth, beginning with the word "tad" (that).
Those whose intellect—consisting of firm conviction—is fixed upon that multitude of qualities such as His lack of partiality;

who are "of that nature" (*tad-ātmānaḥ*), meaning their minds are absorbed in Him; who are "established in Him" (*tan-niṣṭhāḥ*), meaning they have Him as their sole purpose; who are "devoted to Him" (*tat-parāyaṇāḥ*), meaning they take refuge in Him.

Thus, by means of the knowledge of the qualities such as the absence of imbalance in that [state], which has been practiced, those whose impurities have been shaken off and whose aversion to it has perished attain liberation, which is non-return. //17//
The wise perceive with an equal eye a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste. (5.18)
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry as to what kind of wise ones (*jñānin*) go to the state of non-return, he says, "endowed with learning and humility" (*vidyā-vinaya-saṃpanna*).
Those whose nature it is to perceive even in uneven circumstances Brahman alone as equal are the learned;
that is to say, they are the wise.

In this context, there is a disparity based on action (karman) in the case of "a Brāhmaṇa endowed with knowledge and discipline" and "a dog-cooker (śvapāka), who cooks a dog"; and a disparity based on birth (jāti) is shown in the case of "a cow, an elephant, and a dog. //18//
Madhusūdana:

Having described the fruit of knowledge as the state of disembodied liberation (*videha-kaivalya*) after the fall of the body, he now states that its fruit is the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which exists even while the body remains due to the force of *prārabdha*-karma, in the verse beginning with "Knowledge" (*vidyā*).
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers either to the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedas or to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Discipline (*vinaya*) means the absence of egoism, which is to say, the absence of arrogance. In one who is endowed with these two—namely, a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), a disciplined person (*vinīta*), a Brāhmaṇa, and one of the most excellent *sattvic* nature—as well as in a cow that is devoid of refinement, belonging to the *rājasic* and middling category; [in both of these, the quality of Brahman is equal].
Likewise, even toward an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste (śvapāka)— the lowest of all and characterized by extreme darkness—
those whose nature it is to see Brahman equally, untouched by qualities such as *sattva* and the like, or by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from them, are "seers of equality" (*sama-darśinaḥ*);
they are the wise, the possessors of knowledge.
Just as the sun reflected in the waters of the Ganges, in a pond, in wine, or in urine has no connection with the qualities or defects of those [media],
so too Brahman, being reflected through the medium of the *cidābhāsa*, has no connection with the qualities or defects residing in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); thus they reflect upon it.
The meaning is that, by perceiving all things with an equal vision, free from attachment and aversion, they experience liberation while living through the manifestation of supreme bliss. //18//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, for those who have transcended the *guṇas* and do not wish to grasp any distinction consisting of gradation within the mere object composed of the *guṇas*, there can only be equanimity of mind; thus he says, "knowledge" (*vidyā*). [The term] "in a Brāhmaṇa" and "in a cow" is used because they belong to the *sāttvika* class.

In an elephant, in a dog, and in an outcaste (śvapāka)—that is, even in the lowest [beings] due to their being born of *tamas*—the wise who see with equanimity do not perceive those respective distinctions; thus they have transcended the *guṇas*.
Indeed, this very non-perception of distinctions is the equanimous Brahman that has transcended the *guṇas*.
Those whose nature it is to see that [are "those who have the habit of seeing that"]. //18//
Baladeva praises them with the words "vidyā" (knowledge) and so forth:
among such a Brāhmaṇa and even a dog-cooker, these two are unequal by virtue of their actions; and among a cow, an elephant, and a dog, they are unequal by virtue of their birth.
Thus, among those created in such inequality, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, those who perceive the Supreme Self as equal—
They alone are the wise;
their creation proceeds accordingly with that very karma, and not in accordance with passion or hatred. Thus, the Supreme Self is equal toward all, like the rain-cloud. //18//
Even here in this world, rebirth is conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity;
for Brahman is faultless and equal, and therefore they are established in Brahman. (5.19)
Śrīdhara: But how can those who perceive equality in things that are unequal be considered wise, even though they perform such acts?
As Gautama has said: "By these two, one makes the equal unequal and the unequal equal through honor.
The meaning of this is: when one treats the equal with honor in an unequal manner, and treats the unequal with equal honor, that person is deprived of both this world and the next.
Regarding this, he says "right here" (ihaiva). "Right here" means by those very [beings] while they are still living. "Sarga" means creation; it is saṃsāra.
He is conquered and cast out by whom? By those whose mind is established in *sāmya*, in equanimity.
The reason for this is: because Brahman is equal and faultless, therefore those who perceive with equality are established in Brahman alone.

The meaning is that they have attained the state of Brahman (*brahma-bhāva*). However, the fault mentioned by Gautama applies only prior to the attainment of the state of Brahman, because [the scripture] mentions the state of the worshipper (*pūjaka*) in the passage beginning with "from worship" (*pūjātaḥ*). //19//
Madhusūdana:
But surely, the perception of equality among living beings whose natures are inherently unequal—being classified as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*—is forbidden by the Dharmaśāstras.

Thus, Gautama, having begun with the statement that "his food is not to be eaten," records: "One who is equal to these two [the outcaste and the king] is equal to them even when they are unequal in honor."
"Samāsam" is the dative dual;

"viṣamasama" is the locative singular by virtue of the singular form used for a dvandva compound. [This refers to] the kind [of gift] consisting of the giving of clothing, ornaments, food, and so forth, preceded by [the honoring of] those who have mastered the four Vedas and possess exemplary conduct.

A special form of worship is performed for one who is equal to him— namely, one who has mastered the four Vedas and possesses virtuous conduct— if, however, a mode of worship inferior to that [standard] is performed for someone unequal to him;
likewise, for those with little Vedic knowledge and poor conduct, a mode of worship is performed with inferior materials for one who is similarly unequal to them.

The meaning is that when a mode of worship equal to the primary worship is performed for one who is inferior to the previously mentioned Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and follow right conduct—namely, by performing a worship superior to what is due to such an inferior person—the food of that worshipper becomes unfit to be eaten because of honoring the superior as inferior and the inferior as superior. Furthermore, there is another fault: the worshipper, by failing to observe the proper distinction [in conduct], is deprived of both wealth and merit.

Although for ascetics who possess no belongings, the state of having food unfit for consumption and the lack of wealth exist by their very nature due to the absence of cooking and the absence of riches, nevertheless, the fault of the loss of dharma certainly occurs.
Furthermore, the state of having food unfit for consumption is indicative of the production of sin through impurity.

Since austerity is indeed the wealth of those whose wealth is austerity, its loss is certainly a defect; thus, one might ask how those who see with equanimity can be called wise and liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). To this, he replies: "Right here.

By those wise ones who see with equanimity, "creation" (*sarga*)—so called because it is produced (*sṛjyate*)—that is, the phenomenal world of duality, has been conquered and transcended even "right here," in this very state of life.
If so, what need is there to mention that it must be transcended after the fall of the body?
By whom?
By those whose mind is established in equanimity—that is, steady and unwavering—in the state of sameness toward Brahman, even while existing amidst all beings who are inherently unequal.
For since Brahman is faultless, equal, devoid of all modifications, immutable, eternal, and one, therefore they are established in Brahman alone.
This is the meaning:
for defectiveness occurs in two ways—either through connection with something defective despite being non-defective itself, or through being defective by its own nature;
as, for example, the water of the Gaṅgā [becomes defective] by falling into a pit of urine.
Or [it may be] by itself, as in the case of urine and the like.

In that regard, although Brahman—residing in those who possess defects, such as dog-cookers—is perceived by the deluded as being defiled by defects, Brahman remains entirely untainted by all defects because it is unattached, like space.
For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached.
Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by external ocular defects,
so too is the one inner self of all beings.
"Nor is it stained by worldly suffering, for it is external"—so says the Śruti.

Nor is it defiled by itself through the possession of qualities such as desire, since it is established by both Śruti and Smṛti that desire and the like are attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Therefore, the claim that ascetics who are of the nature of the flawless Brahman and are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) are nevertheless tainted by defects such as eating food unfit for consumption is a contradiction.
But the Smṛti rule refers exclusively to ignorant householders,
because it begins with the statement "his food may be eaten," and because it mentions [the guest] in the middle as one who has been "honored."
And it should be understood that this is because of the concluding statement: "He is deprived of both wealth and merit. //19//
Viśvanātha:
He praises the state of equanimity (sama-dṛṣṭitva). Right here, in this very world, "creation" (sarga)—meaning saṃsāra—is conquered, that is, overcome. //19//
Baladeva says: "Here" means in this very state of practice, *sarga*—that is, *saṃsāra* (transmigratory existence)—has been conquered and overcome by them.
By whom? By those whose minds are established and fixed in equanimity (*sāmya*), which is the attribute of Brahman known as freedom from partiality (*avaiṣamya*).
From where does the lack of inequality in Brahman arise?
To this he says: "For [it is] faultless," and so on.

Since they have ascertained that there is no inequality and the like in Brahman, therefore, even while remaining within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), they are in fact established in Brahman alone; the meaning is that liberation is easily attained by them. //19//

One who has attained steadiness of intellect and is undeluded, the knower of Brahman established in Brahman, does not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant, nor does he become agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant. (5.20)
Śrīdhara: He states the characteristic of one who has attained Brahman with the words "na prahṛṣyet" (he should not rejoice).

One who, having become a knower of Brahman, remains established in Brahman alone, should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant—that is, he should not experience excessive joy—and he should not be agitated upon encountering what is unpleasant; the meaning is that he does not despond.
For he whose intellect is steady—meaning his intellect is firm and unwavering—from what cause is that? Because he is undeluded, meaning his delusion has ceased. //20//
Madhusūdana:

Since Brahman is faultless and equal, therefore, one who realizes the Self as having that very form says, "one should not rejoice. The first half of this verse—*with a mind undisturbed by sorrows, and free from longing amidst joys*—has already been explained.

The two suffixes (*liṅ* and *pratyaya*) are used to express that the very natural conduct of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) should be practiced with effort by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

The meaning is that for one whose nature is the vision of the non-dual Self, joy and dejection—which are caused by the attainment of what is pleasant or unpleasant—cannot arise, as such things are external to him.

He explains this very vision of the non-dual Self: "of steady intellect" (*sthira-buddhiḥ*), meaning his intellect is steady and unwavering through the ripening of inquiry into the Vedānta texts preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

One whose intellect regarding Brahman is free from doubt and is certain by virtue of being devoid of all uncertainty—that is to say, one who has attained the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).

Even for such a person, although they are free from all forms of improbability (*asaṃbhāvanā*), direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) does not arise due to the obstruction of contrary mental impressions (*viparīta-bhāva*); therefore, the text speaks of "constant meditation" (*nididhyāsana*)—namely, "one who is undeluded" (*asaṃmūḍhaḥ*).

Through the maturation of constant meditation, which consists of a continuous flow of similar mental impressions uninterrupted by dissimilar ones, one becomes free from the delusion known as contrary mental impressions.
Then, due to the removal of all obstructions, the knower of Brahman becomes one who has direct realization of Brahman.

Consequently, through the ripening of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he remains established in Brahman alone—which is faultless and equanimous—and not elsewhere; thus, "established in Brahman" means one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and possessed of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*).
Since such a person lacks the perception of duality, it is entirely appropriate that joy and agitation do not arise for him.
The intention is that even while dualistic perception persists for the practitioner, joy and dejection must be abandoned through such means as perceiving the defects inherent in sense objects. //20//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, he states their equanimity even toward worldly likes and dislikes with the words "he should not rejoice. "He should not rejoice" means he does not rejoice.
"He should not be agitated" or "he does not become agitated.
Alternatively, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used with the intention of stating that one should practice in this manner during the stage of spiritual discipline (*sādhana-daśā*).
One who is undeluded (*asaṃmūḍha*), because joy, sorrow, and so forth are merely delusion (*saṃmoha*) since they are rooted in egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*). //20//
Baladeva: He states the characteristic of one established in Brahman with the words "not" (na).
Abiding in the present body, having encountered what is pleasant or unpleasant drawn forth by *prārabdha* karma, he should neither rejoice nor be agitated.
Why? Because his intellect is steady within his own Self (*svātman*).
Being undeluded, he does not fall into delusion by identifying the eternal Self with the impermanent body;
such a knower of Brahman, experiencing Brahman in that manner, should be understood as one who is established in Brahman, characterized in this way. //20//
One whose self is unattached to external contacts finds that happiness which is within the self; with his self disciplined by the yoga of Brahman, he enjoys imperishable happiness. 21.
Śrīdhara: He states the cause for the stability of the intellect through the cessation of delusion in the verse beginning with "bāhya-sparśeṣu.
"Sparśas" (contacts) are the objects that are touched by the senses. One whose self—that is, whose mind—is unattached to these objects of the external senses is "asaktātmā."
He finds—that is, he obtains—that sattvic happiness which consists of tranquility within the self, that is, within the internal organ (antaḥ-karaṇa).

And having obtained that happiness of tranquility, he whose self is joined with Brahman through yoga, that is, through meditative absorption (samādhi), and has attained oneness with It, enjoys—that is, he attains—imperishable happiness. //21//
Madhusūdana:

Now, since attachment to external objects has been experienced throughout many lifetimes and is therefore exceedingly powerful, how could one whose mind is attached to them remain fixed upon the transcendental Brahman, which is devoid of all perceived pleasure?

If it is argued that this is because [the mind] has the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), we say no; for since that bliss is something never before experienced, it lacks the capacity to serve as a cause for the stabilization of the mind.
As it is said in the *Vārttika*:
"Even if Ānanda has been heard of directly, if he has not been made an object of direct perception, he is not even capable of diminishing one's longing for the seen Ānanda.
To this, he says: "External," and so forth.
The objects of touch (*sparśa*) are sound and so forth, because they are touched by the sense faculties.
And these are external because they are not of the nature of the self (*anātma-dharma*).

One whose self is unattached—meaning one whose mind is unattached and who is dispassionate due to being empty of craving—finds that bliss which consists of tranquility within the self, that is, within the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*), independent of external objects.
One attains [this] through the activity of a stainless being.
As it is said in the *Bhārata*:
"Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is in heaven..."
"These [other pleasures] do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving"— thus it is said.

Alternatively, that very bliss which is the essential nature of the inner self, the referent of the word "thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*), which is experienced in deep sleep but is not attained due to the obstruction of attachment to external objects— that same bliss one attains through the absence of such attachment.

He states that one does not obtain merely the bliss of the meaning of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-pada), but rather the full bliss through the experience of identity with the meaning of the word "that" (tat-pada): "he whose self— the internal organ— is joined with, or engaged in, yoga— namely samādhi— in Brahman, the Supreme Self, being free from thirst for other objects, is one whose self is joined with the yoga of Brahman."

Alternatively, [the compound may be analyzed as follows]: he whose self (ātman)—that is, the referent of the term *tvaṃ*—is joined with, or has attained oneness with, Brahman—the referent of the term *tat*—through yoga, which is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) consisting of the experience of the meaning of the sentence; such a person "attains" (*aśnute*), that is, pervades, inexhaustible and infinite bliss that constitutes his own essential nature. The meaning is that he exists at all times as the very experience of bliss.
Although the reality is eternal, the connection with the root-meaning [of the verb √aś, "to eat"] is figurative, intended to signify the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, one who desires to experience imperishable bliss within the self should withdraw the senses from the pleasure of external objects—which is momentary and leads to the experience of great hells; for by that alone does one become established in Brahman. This is the intended meaning. //21//
Viśvanātha:
And he, whose self is unattached—that is, whose mind is unattached—to external touches, which are the pleasures of sense-objects;
the reason for this is that when one finds the Supreme Self within the individual self (jīvātman), the happiness that is attained therein is imperishable happiness.
He alone enjoys, that is, attains [this state];
for the sense is that one who has tasted the nectar of immortality without interruption does not find pleasure in clay. //21//
Baladeva: He says "bāhya" etc., meaning that one experiences one's own self and the Supreme Self in a sequence of priority and posteriority.

Being one whose mind is unattached to external touches—that is, to the experiences of objects such as sound—one first finds the happiness that is experienced when one's own essential nature (svasvarūpa) is realized.

Subsequently, being one whose self is joined with yoga, namely samādhi, in the Brahman which is the Supreme Self, one enjoys—that is, obtains—that imperishable happiness characterized by the great experience [of the Absolute]. //21//
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed the wombs of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them. 5.22
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if even the enjoyment of beloved objects ceases, how can liberation (mokṣa) be the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha)? To this he says: "For those... etc.
"Contacts" (saṃsparśāḥ) are the sense-objects; the enjoyments (bhogāḥ), which are pleasures, are those born from them.
For even in the present time, because they are pervaded by rivalry, envy, and so forth, they are the very sources—the causes—of suffering.
Likewise, they have a beginning and an end.
Therefore, the person of discrimination does not take delight in them. //22//
Madhusūdana:

Now, one might object that if the cessation of attachment to external objects results in the experience of imperishable bliss within the Self, and if that experience of bliss results from the very cessation of attachment to external objects, then—due to the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya)—neither of the two would be established. Anticipating this objection:
He states the solution— that the cessation of attachment to those [objects] occurs precisely through the practice of perceiving the defects of sense objects— with the words "For indeed" (*ye hi*).

For indeed, those enjoyments born of contact— arising from the connection between the sense organs and their objects— which are experiences of trifling fragments of pleasure, whether in this world or the next, are nothing but sources of suffering because they are pervaded by passion, hatred, and so forth.
All of these, up to the world of Brahmā, are indeed causes of suffering.
As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"To whatever extent a living being forms mental attachments to things dear to the mind..."
"Into his heart, as many spikes of grief as these are driven.
Such things are not stable, but rather possess a beginning and an end.

The beginning is the contact of the sense organs with their objects, and the end is their separation from them; those things which have these two [beginning and end] appear like a dream in the interval between the prior and subsequent non-existence—momentary and illusory.
This has been stated by the teacher Gauḍapāda: "That which exists at the beginning and at the end also exists likewise in the present.
Since this is so, the wise person who possesses discernment does not delight in those [objects], because they are experienced as disagreeable, and thus he does not experience pleasure in them.

This was stated by the venerable Patañjali: "To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering due to the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and due to the conflict between the functions of the guṇas" (Yogasūtra 2.15).
All sensory pleasure, whether perceived through direct experience or heard of from tradition, is indeed nothing but suffering because it is felt as disagreeable;
this is so for the discerning person who has thoroughly understood the nature of the afflictions and other such factors, but not for the undiscerning.
For the wise man is like the eye-ball, being agitated even by a minute fragment of suffering, just as an extremely delicate wool-thread [is easily broken].

Just as a drop of water placed in the hollow of an eye causes pain through touch, but not so in other parts of the body; likewise, for one who possesses discernment (*vivekin*), every means of enjoyment is suffering because it is permeated by affliction throughout the three periods of time—like eating food mixed with honey and poison—but not for the fool who endures manifold sufferings.
In this context, "by the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions" refers to the past, present, and future times.
Furthermore, because it is permeated by suffering, the state of being suffering is said to belong to sensory pleasure by way of its limiting conditions (*aupādhika*);
and by the phrase "due to the conflict of the functions of the qualities" (*guṇa-vṛtti-virodhāt*), its state of being suffering is shown even by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
In this context, the meaning is: "by those [factors] which are transformation (*pariṇāma*), pain (*tāpa*), and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—these alone being the sufferings."
The third case ending is used here in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).
For instance, every experience of pleasure is indeed permeated by passion;
for it is impossible that one should not be attached to something and yet be happy because of it.
Furthermore, passion itself, having first arisen, transforms into the form of pleasure through the attainment of its objects.
Yet, because it increases at every moment, the suffering caused by the non-attainment of those very objects becomes unavoidable; thus, [passion] is in essence nothing but suffering.
For that which is the subsiding of the senses regarding enjoyments due to complete satisfaction—that is true happiness.

That lack of tranquility which arises from greed is suffering. Furthermore, it is not possible to achieve freedom from craving through the repeated indulgence of the senses; for, following the practice of indulgence, passions increase and the faculties become more skillful. And thus says the Smṛti:
"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.

Therefore, because it is a transformation of passion which is itself of the nature of suffering, sensual pleasure is indeed suffering, since cause and effect are non-different; this is the "suffering of transformation" (pariṇāma-duḥkhatva).
Likewise, at the time of experiencing pleasure, one hates those things adverse to it that are the causes of suffering;
and since enjoyment is not possible without harming living beings, one injures those beings.
Furthermore, hatred is a specific mental resolve (saṅkalpa) characterized by the thought: "May all these causes of suffering never be mine."
And no one at all is able to avoid them all;
therefore, even at the time of experiencing pleasure, because aversion toward its obstacle is always present, the suffering of heat is indeed difficult to avoid.
For heat is indeed aversion.
Thus, one who is unable to avoid the means of suffering becomes deluded; therefore, the state of suffering consisting of delusion (moha-duḥkhatā) must also be explained.
And so it has been stated by the authors of the *Yoga-bhāṣya*: "The experience of pain for everyone is dependent upon means that are sentient or insentient and is permeated by aversion.
In this regard, there exists a latent deposit of karma born of aversion (*dveṣaja-karmāśaya*).

Seeking the means to happiness, one moves through body, speech, and mind; thereafter, one either benefits or harms others, and through these acts of benefiting or harming others, one accumulates merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). It is not that the latent predispositions of karma arise solely from greed or delusion; this is what is called the "suffering of the nature of affliction" (*tāpa-duḥkhatā*).
Thus, a present experience of pleasure, at the time of its own destruction, deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); that [impression] produces the recollection of pleasure,
and that [recollection] produces passion (*rāga*).
The activity of mind, body, and speech; the latencies of meritorious and non-meritorious karma;
and birth and so forth—these constitute the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
In this same way, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of heat and delusion are also to be explained.

Having thus stated that sensory pleasure is indeed suffering because it is permeated by suffering throughout the three periods of time, he now declares its nature as suffering even in its own essence: "And because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*.
The *guṇas*—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; although they possess mutually contradictory natures, [they coexist].

Just as oil, a wick, and fire together initiate a single effect— the lamp— by being utilized for human enjoyment, so too this single effect, though composed of the three *guṇas*, is designated by a single *guṇa* alone through the application of the term "predominant" (*pradhāna*), because when one is predominant, the other two become subordinate (*guṇa-bhāva*). Thus, the effect, although consisting of the three *guṇas*, is designated as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or *tāmasa*.

In that regard, even a cognition in the form of the experience of pleasure, although it is an effect of the manifest *sattva*, is nonetheless composed of all three *guṇas* because it is also an effect of the unmanifest *rajas* and *tamas*.

Thus, just as it possesses the nature of pleasure, it necessarily possesses the nature of pain and the nature of despondency; therefore, for the discerning person, everything is indeed nothing but pain.
Furthermore, even such a cognition is not stable.
Since it is said that the mind is "mobile" because the activity of the *guṇas* is mobile—that is, subject to rapid transformation—one might ask:
how can a single cognition simultaneously experience pleasure, pain, and delusion, which are mutually contradictory? This is not so;
for there is no contradiction between that which is manifest and that which is unmanifest.
For contradiction occurs only between qualities that possess equal activity, not those with unequal activity.

For example, virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and power (*aiśvarya*)—when they have attained their activity—are contradicted by vice (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), passion (*avairāgya*), and lack of power (*anaiśvarya*) only when these latter have likewise attained their activity, and not while merely existing in their own nature.
This is indeed the principle: there is contradiction between a primary [quality] and another primary, but not with one that is weak.
In this same way, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* also cannot coexist simultaneously as primary factors, yet they do not cease to exist altogether.

By this, the simultaneous existence of passion (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*) within the sufferings of transformation, pain, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is also explained; for the afflictions (*kleśas*) have four states—namely, dormant, attenuated, interrupted, and active—and thus ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), passion, aversion, and the clinging to life (*abhiniveśa*) constitute the five afflictions.
Ignorance (avidyā) is the field for the subsequent [afflictions], whether they be dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active.
Ignorance is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self.
The identification of the power of the seer and the power of seeing as a single essence is egoism (asmitā).
Attachment is that which underlies pleasure;
aversion is that which underlies suffering;
and clinging is that which flows spontaneously and is so firmly established as to persist even in the wise.
These subtle [afflictions] are to be abandoned by re-absorption;
their active manifestations are to be abandoned by meditative absorption.
The latent deposit of karma, which has the afflictions as its root, is to be experienced in either the present or a future birth.
"When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience"—these are the *Pātañjala* sūtras (*Yoga Sūtra* 2.13).
In this context, "error" (*viparyaya*), "false knowledge" (*mithyājñāna*), and "ignorance" (*avidyā*) are synonyms for the cognition of something as what it is not.
Its specific manifestation is the cause of *saṃsāra*.
In that regard, the perception of permanence in what is impermanent is as follows: "The earth is eternal; the sky with its moon and stars is eternal; the celestial dwellers are immortal.
The perception of purity in what is impure and utterly loathsome—the body—is as follows: "This lovely girl is like a fresh crescent moon;
she appears as if fashioned from the very essence of honey and nectar, as if she emerged after piercing through the moon, her eyes as long as the petals of a blue lotus."
With what is there a connection for whom that "she seems to console the world of living beings with her eyes full of amorous gestures"?
[The answer is: From the place, from the seed, from the support, from the outflow, and even from the destruction.
For the wise know the body to be impure, because its purity is merely that which is placed upon it.
And such is the verse of Vyāsa’s son.
By this, the notion of merit in what is non-meritorious and the notion of purpose in what is purposeless are explained.

The perception of pleasure in pain has been illustrated; moreover, because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and due to the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person.
The manifestation of the self in what is not-self—such as "I am a man" with respect to the body—is ignorance (*avidyā*); being the root of all afflictions, it is called darkness (*tamas*).
The conceit of non-difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*) is self-identification (*asmitā*), which is delusion (*moha*).

Attachment (*rāga*) is a specific type of misconception (*viparyaya-viśeṣa*) characterized by the thought, "May everything of the nature of happiness be mine," even for one who lacks the means to achieve it;
that itself is great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
Hatred (*dveṣa*) is a specific type of misconception characterized by the thought, "May no suffering whatsoever be mine," even when the causes of suffering are present.
That is *tāmisra*.

Even in the absence of [future] life, the innate and universal fear of death— common to all living beings from the learned man down to women and children— which takes the form of the misconception (*viparyaya*) that "may I not be separated from these impermanent bodies, senses,
and so forth," is *abhiniveśa*.
That is *andhatāmisra*.
As it is said in the Purāṇa:
"Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and that which is designated as *andha*."
"This ignorance of the Great Self has appeared with five sections.
And these afflictions (kleśas) exist in four states.
Among them, the state of sleep is their abiding in an unmanifest form due to the non-arising of that which does not yet exist.
The state of *tanu* (subtle) is the non-production of an effect by that which has been manifested, due to the lack of acquisition of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
The state of *viccheda* (interruption) is the suppression of that which has been manifested and has produced an effect by some powerful factor.
The state of *udāra* (exalted) is the performance of its own effect by that which has been manifested and has attained the full complement of auxiliary causes, without obstruction.

For these four afflictions (*kleśa*), such as egoism (*asmitā*) and the rest, which are characterized by the four states and consist of error (*viparyaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is the common form, the field, and the ground of their production;
for it has been shown that all of them possess the nature of error. Therefore, the meaning is that the cessation of the afflictions occurs precisely through the cessation of ignorance.
And those afflictions are dormant as they are for those who are naturally absorbed in ignorance;
they are attenuated through the cultivation of counteractive measures as they are for yogins.
Both of these types, being subtle, are to be abandoned only by means of withdrawal—the cessation of the mind—through seedless samādhi.

However, those which have subtle functions and are effects thereof— namely, the gross ones— are called "interrupted" (*vicchinna*) because they appear again and again in various forms after having been repeatedly interrupted.
For example, at the time of passion, anger, though present, is said to be "interrupted" because it has not manifested.

Thus, when Caitra is attached to one woman, he is not necessarily detached from others; rather, his attachment toward one has attained its manifestation (*labdha-vṛtti*), while toward others it will attain its manifestation (*bhaviṣyad-vṛtti*). In that case, it is said to be "interrupted.
Those [passions] which have attained their manifestation toward objects are then said to be "manifest" (*prādurbhūta*) and "exalted" (*udāra*) in every respect.

Both of these types, because they are exceedingly gross, are to be abandoned through meditation on the Blessed One by means of the state of pure goodness (*śuddha-sattva-bhāva*); they do not require the restraint of the mind (*mano-nirodha*).
However, those [afflictions] to be abandoned through cessation are indeed subtle.
Thus, all afflictions exist at all times within the sufferings of transformation, pain, and conditioning, in the form of dormant, attenuated, or interrupted states;
the distinction is that they become gross only occasionally for some individuals.
And these, by producing suffering characterized by affliction, become denotable by the term "kleśa" (afflictions);
for the latent impression of karma, known as dharma and adharma, has its root solely in the afflictions.

And when the affliction (*kleśa*), which serves as the root, exists, there is the maturation (*vipāka*)—the fruit—of that latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*), namely birth, lifespan, and experience.
Furthermore, that latent deposit of karma, by initiating its own maturation both in this life and in another, is to be experienced in a visible or an invisible birth.
Thus, the continuum of afflictions revolves incessantly like a waterwheel.
Therefore, it has been rightly said: "Those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering and possess a beginning and an end.

Their being sources of suffering arises from transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth, while their having a beginning and an end arises from the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas* and the instability of those *guṇa*-functions; such is the explanation according to the Yoga system.
For the followers of the Upaniṣads, however, ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless non-existence (*abhāva*) in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva*).

The superimposition of the nature of the Self upon the ego is *asmitā*. Attachment, aversion, and the will to live are specific modifications of those [mental states]. Because they are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), all of them are false by virtue of being of the nature of ignorance, like the superimposition of a snake on a rope. Although they are false, they are sources of suffering; and because they are merely creations of perception, like dreams and so forth, they have a beginning and an end.
Thus, the wise person, having realized the substratum and thereby ceased from delusion, does not take delight in those [objects];

like one who knows the true nature of a mirage and does not proceed toward it seeking water, he understands that there is not even a trace of fragrance of happiness in saṃsāra, and thus he should withdraw all his senses from it—this is the meaning. //22//
Viśvanātha:
He says "ye hi" (for those who) to show that in reality, only one possessed of discernment (*viveka*) becomes attached to the pleasure derived from sense objects. //22//

Baladeva: He says "ye hi" (for those... because one does not become attached to the enjoyment of sense-objects when drawn by unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), due to the certain realization of their impermanence.
"Born of contact" (*saṃsparśajāḥ*) means enjoyments or pleasures produced by sense-objects.
The rest is clear. //22//
He who is able to withstand here, even before liberation from the body, the impulse arising from desire and anger— that man is disciplined and happy. (5.23)
Śrīdhara: Since liberation alone is the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha),
and since the force of desire and anger is its most formidable obstacle,
he says "he is able" to indicate that only one capable of enduring these is a partaker of liberation.
Whatever impulse arises from desire or from anger, characterized by the agitation of the mind, the eyes, and so forth—
the person who is able to endure and restrain that very impulse right here, at the very moment it arises, and not merely for a single instant; [that person is one who has conquered the senses].
But prior to the liberation from the body—
that is, until the fall of the body—
he who is thus constituted alone becomes disciplined, composed, and happy.
It is not otherwise;

or rather, just as after death one endures the force of desire and anger while being empty of life— even though embraced by weeping young women and even while being cremated by sons and others— so too does one endure it while still living before death.
The meaning is that he who endures [these] alone is disciplined and happy.
As it was said by Vasiṣṭha:
"Just as when the life-breath has departed, the body experiences neither pleasure nor pain,"
If that were so, then even one endowed with vital breath would become a locus for absolute liberation. //23//
Madhusūdana says:

"This most grievous defect, which is the cause for the attainment of all misfortune, difficult to restrain, and the adversary of the path to the highest good, must be warded off with great effort by one desiring liberation; thus, in order to enjoin an increase of effort, he speaks again [in the verse beginning] with 'he is able'."

When things favorable to oneself—causes of pleasure—are perceived or remembered, that greed, longing, or thirst consisting of attachment which arises through the habitual contemplation of their qualities is *kāma*. However, the word *kāma* is used in its most established sense for the mutual sexual desire between a man and a woman. In the verse beginning "By this longing, desire (*kāma*), anger, and likewise greed (*lobha*)," desire refers to thirst for wealth (*dhana-tṛṣṇā*) as greed, while thirst for sexual union with women is *kāma*; thus, *kāma* and *lobha* are mentioned separately.
In this context, however, the word *kāma* is employed with the intention of referring to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in general; therefore, greed (*lobha*) is not mentioned separately.

Likewise, when things disagreeable to oneself—causes of suffering—are seen or heard, that burning nature of aversion (*dveṣa*), which consists of resentment (*manyu*), arising from the practice of reflecting upon their defects, is anger (*krodha*).

The intensified state (*utkaṭāvasthā*) of these two, which—by virtue of obstructing the recollection of contradictions with worldly convention and the Vedas—consists in being oriented toward activity that contradicts worldly convention and the Vedas, is called "impulse" (*vega*), due to its similarity to the current of a river.

For just as the current of a river, being exceedingly powerful during the rainy season, causes one to fall into a pit and sink, leading one downward even against one's will by obstructing the recollection of contradictions with worldly convention and the Vedas; so too is this state.

Likewise, the force (*vega*) of desire and anger— made exceedingly powerful by the habitual contemplation of sense objects, which is comparable to the rainy season— is indicated by the use of the term "force" (*vega-pada*).

This force, by bringing about a confrontation with what is contrary to worldly and Vedic norms, casts even an unwilling person into the pit of sense objects and causes them to sink into the ocean of *saṃsāra*, leading them downward into the great hells.
And this has been addressed in the verse beginning with "impelled by what" (*kena prayukto 'yam*).

Such a surge (*vega*) arising from desire and anger— consisting of agitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and characterized by various external transformations such as stiffness and perspiration— is unreliable because it may occur at any time due to manifold causes, until the release from the body— that is, up to the very moment of death.

By means of the detachment known as "mastery," which arises from the practice of perceiving the faults that have arisen within, he is able— and indeed capable— of making those [faults] useless by failing to perform actions corresponding to them;
he alone is the disciplined yogin.
He alone is happy,
he alone is a man and a person, because of his accomplishment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
The implication is that any other, being devoted solely to the animal-like traits of food, sleep, fear, and sexual intercourse, is merely a beast in human form.

Regarding the phrase "until liberation from the body," there is another explanation: just as after death one endures the force of desire and anger even while being embraced by lamenting young women and even while being cremated by sons and others— because one is devoid of life-force— even so, he who endures these while still living before death is "yoked" (yukta), and so forth.
In this context, if one were to say that, like death, even in life there is merely the non-arising of desire and anger, then this would be appropriate;
as it was said by Vasiṣṭha:
"Just as when the vital breath has departed, the body does not experience pleasure or pain," [so too should it be here].
"If that were so, even one endowed with life-force (prāṇa) would dwell in the stage of liberation (kaivalya-āśrama).

But here, since the topic at hand is enduring the impulse of desire and anger once they have arisen, the mere non-arising of those two is not the intended illustration; so what is the point of such excessive insistence? //23//
Viśvanātha says:
"Even though he has fallen into the ocean of worldly existence, he alone is the yogi; he alone is happy"—thus he says, "he is able. (23)
Baladeva: He who is able here, even before the release of the body, to withstand the impulse arising from desire and anger—he is disciplined, he is a happy man. (23)
He who finds happiness within, whose recreation is within, and likewise whose light is solely within—
that yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction in Brahman. 24.
Śrīdhara: One does not attain liberation merely by restraining the impulses of desire and anger;
rather, it is one who is "internally blissful"—that is, one for whom bliss exists within the inner self alone.
Not in sense-objects;
he whose pleasure-garden and playground are within, not without;
he whose light and vision are within.
He does not [find delight] in song, dance, and so forth.
Being thus established in Brahman, he attains—that is, reaches—nirvāṇa, which is absorption into Brahman. //24//
Madhusūdana:
It is not the case that people are liberated merely by enduring the impulses of desire and anger;
rather, it is he who is "within" [who is liberated].

One whose happiness consists of his very own nature, being entirely independent of internal or external objects, is "one whose happiness is within" (*antaḥsukha*), meaning he is devoid of the pleasure produced by external objects.

To the question of why there is an absence of external happiness, he says: one whose delight (*ārāma*)—meaning enjoyment or play—is only within the Self (*ātman*) and not in external objects such as women that serve as means to happiness, is "one whose delight is within" (*antarārāma*); the meaning is that, having renounced all possessions, he is devoid of the means for external happiness.

Now, one might object: "Even for an ascetic who has renounced all possessions, since it is possible for worldly pleasure to arise through such things as hearing the sweet songs of cuckoos and other birds, the touch of a gentle breeze, witnessing the rising of the moon and the dancing of peacocks, drinking the exceedingly sweet and cool water of the Gaṅgā, and smelling the fragrance of ketakī flowers—how can he be devoid of external pleasures and their means? To this, he says:
Likewise, he who is "inner-light" (*antar-jyotis*):

just as his happiness is only internal and not through external objects, so too his light—his consciousness—is only within himself in the Self and not through the external senses; he is one devoid of the consciousness of objects such as sound produced by the ears and other organs.
The particle *eva* (only/just) is connected with all three qualifiers.

The meaning is this: because there is an absence of appearances such as sound during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and because even when those [appearances] manifest at the time of emergence (*vyutthāna*), they are determined to be false, it is impossible for pleasure to arise for him through external objects.

That yogin who is thus endowed with the aforementioned qualifications is "composed" (*samāhita*); he attains *brahma-nirvāṇa*—that very state which is Brahman in the form of supreme bliss and is *nirvāṇa* by virtue of being the cessation of imagined duality.
Because the imagined entity has as its very nature the underlying substratum (adhiṣṭhāna),
one attains— through the removal of the veil of ignorance— that which was already eternally attained;
for one is always already become Brahman, and nothing else.
This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman," and according to the principle of Kāśakṛtsna, "on account of abiding. //24//

Viśvanātha: But for one who has transcended worldly existence, the experience of Brahman alone is happiness; thus he says "yaḥ" (he who). He is one for whom happiness exists only within the inner self (*antarātman*), because he delights only within the inner self.
Therefore, he is one for whom the vision of light is within the inner self alone. //24//
Baladeva says: "That which he is able to endure out of love, he describes as 'he who [is within]';
he whose happiness is by means of the Self experienced within, and whose delight (ārāma) is through that very [Self]."

He whose vision is fixed on that very light—such a yogi, a performer of desireless action, having become Brahman and attained his own pure individual nature (jīva-svarūpa), reaches Brahman; he attains the Supreme Self, for through that [vision] alone is liberation (nirvāṇa) obtained. //24//
The seers, whose taints are destroyed, whose doubts are severed, who have controlled their minds, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the nirvana of Brahman. (5.25)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, as for the phrase "what do they obtain":
the sages (ṛṣayaḥ) are those who possess right vision (samyag-darśinaḥ), whose impurities (kalmaṣam) have been destroyed.
Those who delight in the welfare of all beings and possess even a grain of compassion attain the extinction of Brahman, which is liberation. //25//
Madhusūdana,
explaining other means for the knowledge that is the cause of liberation, says "they obtain" (labhante).
First, their impurities are destroyed by sacrifices and other such practices.
Then, through the purification of the internal organ, they become renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), sages capable of discerning subtle reality.
Then, through the maturation of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means, their dualities are severed and all doubts are removed.
Finally, through the maturation of meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*), they become self-controlled, with their minds one-pointedly fixed upon the Supreme Self alone.
And such knowers of Brahman—who, by virtue of not perceiving duality, are devoted to the welfare of all beings and free from violence—attain the liberation of Brahman.
As the Śruti declares: "When for the one who knows, all beings have become the Self alone, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness?"

The plural number is used for the purpose of demonstrating the lack of restriction (aniyama) stated in such scriptural passages as "He who [is the first] of the gods" (tad yo devānām), and so forth. //25//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, he says "they obtain" [in verse 25] to show that many indeed become perfected through these means.
Baladeva: He says "they obtain" to show that many become thus perfected through their practice.
The sages are seers of reality;
they have severed duality and destroyed all doubt.
The rest is clear. //25//
For those ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained,
and who have realized the Self, the extinction into Brahman exists on every side.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "of those free from desire" (kāmety ādi): it refers to ascetics who are renunciants (saṃnyāsins) and are devoid of desire and anger.

For those whose minds are restrained and who have realized the true nature of the Self, there is absorption into Brahman both while living and after death; the meaning is that their dissolution in Brahman does not occur only at the end of the body, but rather exists even while they are alive. //26//
Madhusūdana:

Previously, it was stated that even when desire and anger have arisen, their impulse must be endured; however, now he says "kāma... (desire... to indicate that one must instead prevent their very arising.
"The separation from desire and anger" means precisely their non-arising for those who are already possessed by them—that is, for those who are separated from desire and anger.
Therefore, for those ascetics who possess restrained minds, who are disciplined in heart, who are habituated to effort, who have renounced all worldly ties, and who have realized the Self—
having directly perceived the Supreme Self— the state of Brahman-extinction, which is liberation, exists for them both while they are living and after they have died, because it is eternal.
But it will not [be so], because of the absence of being that which is to be proven (sādhya). //26//
Viśvanātha:

In response to the inquiry as to how long it takes for those who have known the meaning of the term *tvaṃ-pada*—that is, those who have attained knowledge of the Supreme Self—to experience the bliss of Brahman-liberation (*brahma-nirvāṇa*), he says "kāma" and so forth.
This refers to those whose minds are restrained—that is, whose mental faculties have ceased—and whose subtle bodies (*liṅga-śarīra*) have been exhausted.
The sense is that since he exists as one who acts toward [the goal] from every side and in every way, there will be no excessive delay for him in attaining the liberation of Brahman. //26//
Baladeva: He says "kāma" (desire) etc., to show that even the Supreme Self conforms to such [beings].
The meaning is that for those ascetics who possess effort (*yatīnām prayatnavatām*), Brahman exists all around them. As it has been said:
"By means of seeing, meditating upon, and touching, fish, tortoises, and birds [attain their respective goals]."
"They nourish their own offspring; so too do I, O Lotus-born One. (26)
Having placed the external sense objects outside, and having fixed the gaze between the two eyebrows, and having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils; 5.27.
The sage whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained, who is devoted to liberation, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed—he is indeed always liberated. (28)
Śrīdhara: In passages such as "that yogi attains the extinction into Brahman," it is stated that the yogi obtains liberation.
He describes that very yoga in brief with the two verses beginning with "Sparśān" (sensory contacts).
External sensory objects, such as forms, tastes, and so forth, when contemplated, enter within.
Having turned them outward by abandoning those thoughts,
he should fix his gaze between the eyebrows, that is, in the very middle of the brows; for if the eyes are completely closed, the mind dissolves into sleep,
and if they are opened, it wanders outward.
The meaning is that, in order to avoid both those faults, one should fix the gaze between the eyebrows with the eyes half-closed.
Having made the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, which move within the nostrils in the form of inhalation and exhalation, equal by obstructing their upward and downward movements— that is,
having performed *kumbhaka* (breath-retention)— is the sense.

Or rather, having made the two equal by means of slow inhalation and exhalation, such that this prāṇa does not go out excessively and the apāna does not enter too deeply, but both move only within the middle of the nose. //27//
"Yateta": by this means, one whose senses, mind, and intellect are restrained and fully controlled;
one for whom liberation alone is the supreme goal (ayana) to be attained;
and therefore, one from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed.
The meaning is that such a sage, even while living, is always liberated. //27-28//
Madhusūdana:

It has been stated that for one who has previously surrendered all states of being to the Lord, purification of the internal organ arises through the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*); from that follows the renunciation of all actions; and then, for one intent upon hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), which is the means to liberation, arises.

Now, in order to explain in detail the yoga of meditation— which was indicated by the phrase "the yogi attains the nirvana of Brahman" as the internal means for right vision— the Blessed One speaks three verses that serve as the aphorisms (sūtras).
The entire sixth chapter will serve as the commentary (vṛtti) upon these very verses.
Therein, yoga is briefly described by means of two [verses],

while the third [verse] distinguishes its fruit as the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-jñāna*). One should [withdraw] the external objects of touch, such as sound and so forth— which, though existing externally, enter through the doors of the ears and other senses via the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) assuming their respective forms.

The meaning is: having again made those which had entered within external, without producing any mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of this or that [object] due to the power of supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*).
If these were internal, they would not become external even by a thousand means, because it would entail the destruction of their own nature (*svabhāva-bhaṅga*).
However, the qualification "external" (bāhyān) is used to state that for those who have entered within under the influence of passion, it is possible to go outside through dispassion (vairāgya).

Having thus stated dispassion by this, he speaks of practice (abhyāsa), which is connected [to the previous verse] by the phrase "having fixed the gaze between the eyebrows. For if the eyes were completely closed, there would be only one modification (vṛtti), namely sleep, which consists of dissolution (laya).
By extension, however, there would be four fluctuations consisting of distraction—namely, valid cognition, misconception, conceptualization, and memory.
Since all five fluctuations must be restrained, one should place the eyes between the eyebrows with half-closed lids.
Likewise, the prāṇa and apāna breaths should be made equal.
Having made the two [breaths] equal by cutting off their upward and downward movement through retention (*kumbhaka*) so that they move within the nostrils,

one whose senses, mind, and intellect are thus restrained and controlled should become a sage (*muni*)— one habituated to contemplation— who is intent on liberation and detached from all sense objects.
"One whose desire, fear, and anger have departed" has been explained here as "one from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed.
A renunciant who is always such as this is indeed liberated;
for him, there is no liberation yet to be accomplished.
Alternatively, he who is such as this is indeed liberated even while living. //27-28//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, through the yoga of desireless action dedicated to the Lord, there arises purity of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
from that, there arises knowledge concerning the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃ-padārtha).
Therefore, devotion is for the sake of knowing the meaning of that [Supreme] Reality;
it has been stated that through the knowledge arising from that, there is the experience of Brahman by one who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta).

Now, in the sixth chapter, the Lord intends to describe the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) as the means for the experience of Brahman for one whose internal organ is purified by the yoga of action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma-yoga), and which is superior even to the yoga of knowledge (jñāna-yoga); thus, this serves as its introductory aphorism.
He speaks three verses beginning with "sparśān" (objects of touch).
Only external objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are denoted by the term "sparśa";
those which exist having entered into the mind [are likewise included].
Therefore, the meaning is: having withdrawn the mind from external objects by setting it aside from them;
and having placed the two eyes between the eyebrows—that is, in the middle—because when the eyes are fully closed, the mind dissolves in sleep, and when they are opened, it wanders outward;
thus, for the sake of avoiding both these faults, one should keep the eyes half-closed.
Fixing his gaze between the eyebrows, he equalizes the prāṇa and apāna—which move within the nostrils in the form of inhalation and exhalation—by restraining their upward and downward movements;
he is one by whom the senses and other faculties have been brought under control. (27–28)

Baladeva: Now, one whose mind has been purified by desireless action and who has attained self-knowledge should practice *samādhi* for the realization of that [Self]. Thus, indicating *yoga* with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-yoga*), he says "sparśān" (touches).
"Touches" refers to the objects such as sound and so forth; being external, they enter into the mind.
Having cast them out by abandoning the memory of them—that is, having withdrawn the mind from the objects—this is the meaning.

Having fixed the gaze between the two eyebrows, in the middle; for if the eyes are fully closed, there is a dissolution of the mind due to sleep, and if they are opened, there would be an outward diffusion of it. To avoid both of these, the meaning is that one should place the vision between the eyebrows with the eyes half-closed.
Likewise, having made equal—that is, balanced—the *prāṇa* and *apāna* moving within the nostrils by restraining their upward and downward movements, which is to say, having performed *kumbhaka*;
by this means, he is one by whom the senses and so forth have been restrained and established for the sake of beholding the Self;
he is a sage (*muni*), whose nature is the contemplation of the Self.

One who is devoted to liberation has liberation as his sole purpose; therefore, he is free from desire and the like. Such a person is liberated at all times—not only at the time of the fruit, but also during the time of the practice. //27-28//
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. 5.29

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can liberation come about merely by the restraint of the senses and so forth? It does not come by that alone; rather, it is through the medium of knowledge. To this he says: "the enjoyer," and so on.
The enjoyer—or rather, the protector—of sacrifices and austerities offered by My devotees according to their will;
the Great Lord of all worlds;
the friend of all beings, who acts for their benefit without expectation of reward.
Having known me as the inner controller, one attains—reaches—peace, which is liberation, through my grace. //29//
I bow to that Hari, the omniscient one, by whom the combination of Sāṅkhya and Yoga was thus taught in succession, through the removal of doubts regarding conceptual construction.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Renunciation," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana:
To the question, "What must one know who is thus engaged in yoga to be liberated?", he says: "The enjoyer" (bhoktāram).
This refers to Him who, in the form of the agent and in the form of the deity, is the enjoyer, the performer of enjoyment, or the protector of all sacrifices and austerities.
The verbal root *bhuj* has the meanings "to protect" and "to consume.
[He is] the Great Lord of all worlds, the controller even of Hiraṇyagarbha and others;
the friend of all living beings, who benefits them without expectation of anything in return; the inner ruler of all, and the illuminator of everything.

The meaning is that by knowing me, Nārāyaṇa— the one whose sole essence is the fullness of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the self of all— as one's own Self and realizing him directly, one attains peace, which is the cessation of all saṃsāra, that is, liberation (*mukti*).
To dispel the doubt, "Even though I behold you, why am I not liberated?", these qualifying attributes are provided.
The intended meaning is that my knowledge, precisely in the form described above, is the cause of liberation. //29//
The thorough knowledge of one's own true nature, which is brought to perfection through the practice of manifold means and proclaimed by Hari, is the means of liberation for all. (5)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Full Realization of One's Own True Nature," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā), composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:
Even for such a yogi, as for the man of knowledge (jñānin), liberation comes only through the knowledge of the Supreme Self arising from devotion; thus he says, "the enjoyer" (bhoktāram).

He is the enjoyer and protector of sacrifices performed by those engaged in ritual action (karmis) and of austerities performed by those possessed of knowledge; thus, He is the object of worship for both the ritualists and the men of knowledge.

Having known Me as the object of worship for devotees— Me who am the Great Lord of all worlds, the Great Controller, the Inner Ruler worshipped by yogis, the friend of all beings, and the benefactor who acts for their welfare through compassion by means of My own devotees and the instruction of devotion to Me— [one attains Me]; for it is impossible to have an experience of Me, who am beyond all qualities (nirguṇa), by means of knowledge consisting of the quality of goodness (sattva).

From my statement, "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone," the yogi, through that very dispassionate devotion, brings me—the Supreme Self who is his object of worship—within the range of direct perception and attains peace, which is liberation. //29//
Through action performed without desire, the man of knowledge and the yogi are liberated here;
having known both the individual self and the supreme self—this is declared to be the meaning of the chapter.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, the fifth chapter has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous. 5.

Baladeva: Thus, one who is established in samādhi and has realized his own self is said to be the one who worships the Supreme Self; this is stated in the verse beginning with "the enjoyer" (bhoktāram). He is the enjoyer and protector of sacrifices and austerities, and the Great Lord (maheśvara) even of all the worlds, including Brahmā, Rudra, and the others.
Because of such scriptural declarations as, "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among the lords" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7),
one who knows Me to be such— a friend to all beings and an unconditionally beneficent one— and experiences Me as being worthy of worship, attains peace, which is the cessation of saṃsāra.
Indeed, the propitiation of the Lord of All, who is the friend of all, brings happiness and is the means for attaining happiness. //29//
One is liberated through desireless action preceded by yoga;
established in that which contains knowledge as its core—this is the fifth definitive conclusion.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā Upaniṣad. //5//
The Fifth Chapter: The Yoga of Renunciation (Sannyāsa-yoga)
